title: Horne-Francis reveals Nasiah recruitment plan during AFL Origin camp
text:
Jason Horne-Francis is open to throwing his weight around in South Australia's AFL Origin camp to recruit St Kilda superstar and friend Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera.

South Australia and Western Australia today named their first five representatives for next year's Origin match, to be played at Perth Stadium on February 27.

Wanganeen-Milera and Port Adelaide's Horne-Francis were picked by SA coach Craig McRae, along with Saints co-captain Callum Wilkie, Adelaide skipper Jordan Dawson and Collingwood boom recruit Lachie Neale.

Players committed to 2027 AFL Origin SOUTH AUSTRALIA: Jason Horne-Francis, Callum Wilkie, Lachie Neale, Jordan Dawson, Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera WESTERN AUSTRALIA: Patrick Cripps, Charlie Cameron, Kysaiah Pickett, Luke Jackson, Tom Barrass

Wanganeen-Milera rejected massive interest from his native South Australia in 2025 to re-sign on a two-season, $4 million deal with the Saints.

Locking away the silky 23-year-old playmaker on an extension is top of St Kilda's agenda.

This year's Origin revival match between WA and Victoria allowed Western Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli to build a connection with Zak Butters, who crossed from Port Adelaide in the off-season.

While already mates with Wanganeen-Milera, Horne-Francis is mindful of the recruitment opportunity Origin camp presents.

"That worked, didn't it," he told reporters, referring to the Butters-Bontempelli connection developed through Victoria's Origin team.

Marcus Bontempelli (background) successfully recruited Victorian teammate Zak Butters (foreground) to the Western Bulldogs. (Daniel Carson/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

"So maybe I've got to try to do the same thing. Not that we need any more bonding time — we see each other bloody all the time anyway.

"We ran out together in the [Indigenous] All-Stars as well, so it will be good to run out with him again and see what he's got for us."

The 23-year-old admitted he might have to battle with Crows rivals to wrap an arm around Wanganeen-Milera, who finished fourth in St Kilda's best-and-fairest this season.

"There might be a bit of push and shove there," the Port ball-winner said.

St KIlda star Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera is once again in high demand as he comes out of contract. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Horne-Francis and other Adelaide-based SA representatives may have to go through Wilkie to get some alone time with Wanganeen-Milera.

"I won't let him talk to Dawson or anyone from Port," Wilkie joked.

"He'll stay right under my wing.

"Nas is amazing at putting that [contract speculation] to bed and focusing on us and what he brings to the club on field and off field."

Wilkie said he and Wanganeen-Milera had been speaking about the possibility of donning the SA jumper all year.

Collingwood coach Craig McRae will lead Wanganeen-Milera and South Australia in the Origin clash. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"That's what's so special about it," he said.

"You think when you're getting drafted you're never going to be able to pull the colours on again."

WA coach Dean Cox's first selections are Hawthorn defender Tom Barrass, Brisbane forward Charlie Cameron, Carlton skipper Patrick Cripps, Fremantle ruck Luke Jackson and Melbourne livewire Kysaiah Pickett.

Cripps, who captained WA against Victoria this year, is also due to come off contract at the end of next season.

Carlton captain Patrick Cripps has no plans to finish his AFL career in WA. (Getty images/AFL Photos: Matt King)

But the dual Brownlow Medal winner hosed down the possibility of finishing his illustrious career in his home state after the Blues made the finals under now-permanent coach Josh Fraser, despite starting last season 1-8.

"I've been here that long, you sort of become ingrained in the club," Cripps said.

"I sort of feel like a Carlton supporter these days … this is my 14th season.

"I've always loved playing footy at Carlton and been driven to try and build the club from the ground up, and I'm really excited about where we are right now."

AAP

title: India breaks New Zealand Test record with monster innings in Wellington
text:
India has broken the record for the highest Test score in a match played in New Zealand as it put itself in a commanding position to win the first Test in Wellington.

New Zealand reached 2-119 at the close of play on day four as it fought to save the first Test after India declared on a mammoth 9-720 with an imposing first-innings lead of 352.

India's assault was led by Rishabh Pant (128), whose six sixes took his career tally to 108 in just 53 Tests, now second behind all-time best Ben Stokes (138). Pant surpassed former NZ captain Brendon McCullum (107) during the innings.

New Zealand's hopes of a result rest on batting for much of the remainder of the match and forcing a draw, despite losing Tom Latham for a duck and first-innings centurion Henry Nicholls for 31.

Opener Devon Conway, who scored his 22nd Test half-century on his way to an unbeaten 59, and Rachin Ravindra (27 not out) will resume on day five with the Black Caps still 233 runs from forcing India to bat again.

India's pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah (1-33) again made an early breakthrough, sending Latham back on the second ball of the innings, the New Zealand skipper edging behind to take a pair.

Nicholls, whose 175 was the backbone of New Zealand's first-innings 368, got an edge and a bit of thigh pad on a Prasidh Krishna delivery, and Dhruv Jurel showed stunning reflexes to take the catch at short leg.

Jurel had earlier become the sixth batter to score a half-century in India's innings before being caught in the deep for 78, triggering the declaration an hour before tea.

India had resumed on 4-486 on another sunny morning at the Basin Reserve with the clear intent of pushing their 118-run lead out to the sort of tally that would take the possibility of a New Zealand victory out of the equation.

There are few better batters for such a task than Pant, and the swashbuckling wicketkeeper showed the full range of his shots as he approached his ninth Test hundred.

Pant was finally caught on the boundary for 128 off the bowling of Ravindra to bring up lunch, but the punishment for New Zealand continued into the second session.

Jacob Duffy finished with 1-201 off 33 overs. (Getty Images: Hagen Hopkins)

India's final score was well clear of its previous best innings tally in New Zealand of 520 all out in Hamilton in 2009 — a match they won by 10 wickets.

All-rounder Glenn Phillips (3-154) picked a couple of wickets as the Indian batters went for their shots ahead of the declaration to make his figures a bit more respectable.

Seamer Jacob Duffy, though, finished with unenviable figures of 1-201 from his 33 overs, only 28 runs shy of New Zealand's most expensive ever bowling display, which spinner Stephen Boock tallied against Pakistan in 1989.

Reuters

title: 'One-in-2,000-year weather' to be investigated post-blackout
text:
The SA government says the suggestion that a "one-in-2,000-year weather event" was responsible for the Eyre Peninsula blackout will be critically examined amid ongoing fallout from the incident.

Electricity supply to the peninsula and the state's West Coast was cut on Thursday afternoon when two transmission towers collapsed and a third was severely damaged during intense storms, leaving more than 20,000 properties without power.

Power was gradually restored to most of those properties over the following 24 hours, but the blackout has again raised the question of energy security, 10 years on from the 2016 statewide blackout.

ElectraNet — which is responsible for the state's high-energy transmission lines — on Sunday confirmed it was conducting a "complete and thorough review" into the recent outage.

SA's statewide blackout remembered after 10 years Energy policy has changed greatly since South Australia was left in darkness exactly 10 years ago today — but if there is a universal constant of the energy debate, it is that there is always friction over electricity.

On Friday, the company suggested the towers were likely brought down by a "one-in-2,000-year weather event" — a contention SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said would be considered during investigations into the incident.

"There are one of two possibilities here," Mr Malinauskas said.

"Either this was a genuine 'one-in-2,000-year weather event' here that understandably nothing can withstand — or, two, something went wrong in terms of the specifications of that infrastructure.

"That's what the investigation will examine, and that's what we're very keen to look at before we rush to make a judgement."

ElectraNet says two towers were downed and a third sustained major damage. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

The high-voltage transmission line along which the towers collapsed was completed only a few years ago, at a cost of $300 million.

ElectraNet executive Alex Trento told 891 ABC Adelaide on Friday the transmission towers were "built to a one-in-2,000-year weather event", and to withstand wind speeds of up to 172km/h.

"What we think has occurred is that the weather in this localised region has been even stronger than the winds that it was designed for," Mr Trento said.

He said ElectraNet was "always in contact with the bureau" but said there was no advance warning of an event on the scale of what occurred on Thursday.

But he added that what had occurred was "a very unique, very rare occurrence in a very localised area".

"I don't think we could have done anything better from that perspective."

'No evidence of tornadoes'

The Bureau of Meteorology said while wind speeds of around 100km/h were recorded at Roxby Downs on Thursday, gusts of around 170km/h were "unlikely".

"When we're talking wind gusts of more than 170km/h — those are the wind gusts you typically only see in tropical cyclones or associated with tornadoes," senior meteorologist Jonathan How said last week.

"There was no evidence of tornadoes that we could see [on Thursday] across the Eyre Peninsula.

" So certainly, 170km/h is something we couldn't really confirm. It's probably unlikely at this stage because the state record for South Australia is 167km/h. That was set in Woomera back in 1979. "

The images of collapsed and damaged towers at Wharminda on Eyre Peninsula are reminiscent of the scenes that accompanied the 2016 statewide blackout, when towers were felled in the state's mid north.

At a media conference on Friday afternoon, Mr Trento said that following the 2016 event, transmission line design standards were improved.

A fallen transmission tower near Melrose in South Australia in 2016. (ABC News: Dean Faulkner)

Asked whether there was a structural fault in the new towers, Mr Trento conceded that was a possibility, but expressed confidence that the towers had been constructed in accordance with the appropriate standards.

"We are investigating … but at this point in time, seeing the localisation of the event, we do think that the towers have been designed and constructed effectively," he said.

"We think the wind that has entered those towers has been above the specification that we've constructed it to.

"We could have been looking at a 250km/h wind session. We just don't know."

title: Spirit of Tasmania operator told not to use autopilot for entire voyage
text:
Australia's maritime regulator has ordered the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries to stop using autopilot entirely, as a probe into steering issues on one of the vessels continues.

TT-Line previously suspended use of autopilot on the ferries during transits of Victoria's Port Phillip Bay, after the primary steering system on Spirit IV failed during a switch to manual mode.

This restriction has since been expanded to cover the whole Bass Strait voyage following a notice issued by the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), which came into effect on Saturday.

"AMSA stipulated that both vessels are required to stay in hand steering [for the] full voyage," a TT-Line spokesperson said.

"[It is] important to note that there is another primary steering system available on both vessels, and additional back up systems that the crew are fully trained in."

Spirit IV docks late again after 'technical issue' It's the second time this month that the new Spirit of Tasmania ferry has dropped passengers off hours behind schedule. Tracking shows the new vessel spent hours performing loops in Port Philip Bay before being escorted by a tugboat into Geelong.

The directive was the result of an "intermittent fault" on the steering system on Spirit IV, but there was no similar issue on Spirit V, according to the spokesperson.

They said it was expected the directive would be lifted by AMSA as soon as the fault was rectified, and that it would not affect travel times for passengers.

State-owned TT-Line has reached out to Kongsberg Maritime, the Norwegian company that supplied the steering systems for the new vessels.

Technicians will be on site tomorrow to attempt to address the steering issue and the party responsible for funding repairs was "to be determined", the spokesperson said.

Spirit IV being escorted to Geelong by a tugboat earlier this month. (Facebook: Ferries of Tasmania)

Removing the use of automatic steering on the vessels increases the workload for staff, and TT-Line said an extra two crew members would be required to assist each vessel.

Since entering operations late last month, Spirit IV has docked hours late in Geelong because of technical issues on multiple occasions, including on November 5 and November 21.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is investigating the steering issue on Spirit IV, as well as a separate issue on Spirit V which occurred during a trial voyage in October.

AMSA has been contacted for comment.

The new Spirit vessels came into service last month. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

'Teething problems' anticipated

The TT-Line spokesperson described the steering problems as "teething issues" and said they were "regrettable".

"We have said from day one that there will be issues uncovered and dealt with as they are identified," they said.

"The intermittent fault is an example of this, which could only be identified when the vessels entered service."

Tasmanian government minister Bridget Archer said it "was not unreasonable" for the brand new ships to be experiencing some early problems.

"We anticipated there may be some initial teething problems, as we have seen, because of the nature of the scale of these vessels that we're bringing into service," Ms Archer said.

State Labor MP Sarah Lovell said while it was understandable for major infrastructure projects to have teething issues, it was important for the public to be kept in the loop.

"What's important is that the government make sure that these instances are properly investigated and that they're open and transparent … about the causes and what's being done to fix it," Ms Lovell said.

title: Wallabies still have a pulse despite nervous moments in win over Wales
text:
In Les Kiss's words, the Wallabies "earned their corn" with their gritty 29-26 Nations Championship win over Wales in Cardiff.

After ending a four-match losing streak, the Wallabies coach struck a relieved but proud figure when he and captain Harry Wilson fronted the post-match media conference.

It couldn't be described as a polished display on the field, nor was there a moment during the match where it seemed the Wallabies were dominating their opposition.

Each time they opened up an encouraging lead on the scoreboard, it never felt as though Wales was too far away from clawing its way back into the contest.

Wallabies defeat Wales The Wallabies hold on to defeat Wales 29-26 following a thrilling finish to their Nations Championship Test in Cardiff.

But winning breeds confidence, which had been in short supply for the Wallabies following losses to New Zealand (twice), England and Scotland.

"They had to work hard for it and I think tonight was a true Test match [and] they earned their corn and got what they deserved," Kiss said.

An improved defensive effort was among the positives in the Wallabies' performance.

While three of the four tries they conceded came from driving mauls off line-outs, they denied Wales more than once with their scramble defence deep inside the 22.

"When we do it [defence] well, it's a real point of difference for us," Wilson said.

"I thought our D-zone [inside 22] defence tonight was unbelievable."

The Wallabies' aerial game in attack also showed glimpses of its potential, with Max Jorgensen's second-half try an example of the pressure they can apply to opposition teams.

The line-out was strong (they enjoyed a clean sheet on their throw), highlighted by Josh Canham's clutch steal when Wales was camped inside the Wallabies' 22 during the first half.

Wallabies lock Josh Canham (right) enjoyed an excellent all-round performance. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

But the Wallabies let themselves down with poor discipline, especially inside their territory.

They conceded nine penalties in the opening 40 minutes, seven of which were on their side of the halfway line.

By full-time, the Wallabies had given 11 penalties away inside their half, with Wilson shown a yellow card in the 77th minute for one of those indiscretions.

If the Wallabies do the same against Ireland at Twickenham next weekend, they won't be shown any leniency.

Kiss admits the Wallabies' penalty count gave him "the shits".

"Discipline was a little bit disappointing, I must say … it kept them [Wales] in the game with field position and a few things like that," he said.

"So we're going to have to look at that as well."

Ikitau to the fore

Among individual performances, Carter Gordon looked assured at fly half.

The Wallabies were still pedestrian at times with ball in hand, however Gordon did enough to indicate he's the most suitable candidate to wear the number 10 jersey.

Wallabies fly half Carter Gordon looked solid against Wales. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

Len Ikitau was deservedly named player of the match, again proving he's a world-class operator.

But the question remains whether he's better suited to inside or outside centre.

When the Wallabies pulled off their upset 42-38 win over the world champion Springboks in Perth in September, his performance at outside was superb until he left the field injured.

On that occasion, he was partnered in the centres by Hunter Paisami, who is unavailable for the Wallabies' Nations Championship campaign in Great Britain.

Ikitau played inside centre against Wales, with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii admirably slotting in at 13.

Len Ikitau was outstanding in the Wallabies' win. (Getty Images/CameraSport: Ian Cook)

A permanent Ikitau-Paisami midfield combination may be the Wallabies' best option at next year's Rugby World Cup, although Suaalii's stocks at outside centre rose in Cardiff, even though he appears more comfortable on the wing.

For now, the Wallabies will turn their focus to the Ireland Test, which pits the two third-ranked teams from the respective Nations Championship groups against each other.

Their spirits will be buoyed by halting their losing streak, but Kiss knows the pressure of Test rugby never lets up.

"Test match footy doesn't hand you things easy," Kiss said.

title: Bellamy to end Storm coaching stint after 2027 NRL season
text:
Melbourne can officially begin planning for life after Craig Bellamy, after the veteran coach confirmed the longest tenure in NRL premiership history would end in 2027.

After years of speculation about his future, Bellamy will officially finish with the Storm next year at the end of his 25th season in charge of the club.

The 67-year-old's call to walk away comes after he was diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder this year.

Craig Bellamy's coaching CV NRL - Brisbane Broncos (2002): Two matches, one win, one loss

NRL - Melbourne Storm (2003-current): 630 matches, 433 wins, 195 losses, two draws

NRL premierships: 2012, 2017, 2020 (all with Storm)

State of Origin - New South Wales (2008-10): Nine matches, two wins, seven losses

But he still hopes to play some role around the club after 2027, with the five-time premiership-winning coach the most powerful figure in the Storm's history.

"I love this club and everything it represents, the people, our history and our fans," Bellamy said.

"I still have huge passion for the job, and I'm excited about what we can achieve together in 2027.

"While 2027 will be my final season as senior coach, I'm determined to make the most of the opportunity and give everything I can to our club and our players.

"I've always said I'll continue coaching while I believe I can make a positive contribution, and I feel I can still do that.

"I also feel the time is right to make 2027 my final year."

Cameron Munster is one of several big-name Storm stars who are off-contract at the end of the 2027 season. (Getty Images: Pete Dovgan/Speed Media/Icon Sportswire)

Bellamy's decision to officially call stumps comes after chief executive Justin Rodksi admitted on Friday the uncertain future had complicated contract talks with the club's biggest names.

Harry Grant, Cameron Munster and Stefano Utoikamanu are all off-contract at the end of 2027, with the Storm facing an uphill fight to retain all three.

Melbourne hasn't been able to provide clarity on who will coach the club in 2028, unable to officially move on appointing a successor until Bellamy had decided his future.

Billy Slater remains the biggest name linked with Melbourne after he walked away from the Queensland State of Origin job in August.

Billy Slater is the highest-profile name tipped to be Bellamy's successor for the Storm. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Slater does sit on Melbourne's part-time staff, but has so far suggested he does not want to coach in the NRL.

Bellamy also declared in August that Melbourne's next coach should come from within, with Marc Brentnall, Ryan Hinchliffe and Bellamy's son Aaron his full-time assistants.

Brad Arthur, Michael Maguire, Anthony Seibold and Jason Ryles are among coaches to have come out of Bellamy's system in Melbourne.

Arthur is currently coaching Leeds in the Super League, but has signalled a desire to return to the NRL, while Maguire is under pressure at the Broncos.

Ryles is on the verge of signing an extension at Parramatta, while Seibold is a free agent after being sacked by Manly last season.

"Craig is one of the greatest coaches in the history of rugby league, and we're proud of everything he has achieved in the game," Storm chairman Matthew Tripp said.

"We're also delighted he'll have one final season in charge in 2027.

"While we would obviously love to have Craig coaching our team forever, we understand how significant this decision is and are incredibly grateful that we will have another season with him leading our club."

AAP

title: Live: Oscar Piastri snaps at team, climbs from 17th to third in thrilling Vegas GP
text:
— reporting by Reuters

Kimi Antonelli may have already secured the world drivers' championship, but he and Mercedes proved they aren't done yet as the 20-year-old wunderkind posted the fastest qualifying time on Friday ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

However, Antonelli was denied his eighth pole of the season by a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation.

Antonelli had a time of 1 minute, 33.893 seconds, edging out Verstappen by 0.258 seconds in the closing moments of qualifying with a dramatic final lap. Mercedes sent Antonelli out for his final lap with just a second remaining in Q3, which ended up being yet another timely move for the sport's dominant team this season.

"It was very weird qualifying for me," Antonelli said. "First of all, I couldn't get the tyres working, just zero feeling with the car, and also the brake pedal was very long, so I was struggling on the braking. But all in all, it was so unexpected. And that last lap, I thought I was screwed because I started one second from the car in front, but the tow is so big here that I was able to gain with that and put it on pole."

Red Bull needs every break it can get to eclipse Ferrari for second place in the constructors' championship, and it got a couple on Friday. In addition to Verstappen ending up on the pole and Isack Hadjar qualifying in fifth, both Ferraris missed Q3 for the first time since the 2025 Emilia-Romagna Grand Prix, as Charles Leclerc qualified 11th and Lewis Hamilton qualified 12th.

"I think we had a solid qualifying," Verstappen said. "We executed well. My first lap in Q3 was pretty much as good as it can be. I think just with the tow effect as well around the lap, I think (being on) the front row is very good for us."

Mercedes' George Russell qualified third, 0.331 seconds behind Antonelli, but will start alongside Verstappen on the front row.

Lando Norris qualified fourth and Oscar Piastri qualified seventh for McLaren as last year's constructors' champions look to eclipse Red Bull for a third-place finish in the final three races. However, Piastri is facing a 10-place grid penalty for installing a fifth internal combustion engine this season, above F1's limit.

Both Racing Bulls drivers qualified in the top 10, as Arvid Lindblad had the sixth-fastest time and Liam Lawson was the eighth-fastest.

title: Roast chicken sales scrutinised as Coles appeals ACCC's ban on outback store
text:
As the crows flies, Australia's largest outback city is 2,290km from Melbourne and 2,618km from Canberra.

But lawyers and bureaucrats on the other side of the country are having a significant say in how Kalgoorlie-Boulder's residents do their weekly grocery shopping.

The Australian Competition Tribunal this week wrapped eight days of hearings in Melbourne's Federal Court, centred on whether Coles should be permitted to open a new supermarket in the historic gold mining city.

To say some of the 30,000-strong population are annoyed at the prospect would be an understatement.

Doug Daws has lived in Kalgoorlie-Boulder his entire life. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Kalgoorlie-Boulder's former Deputy Mayor Doug Daws is among them.

"If you want to spend money in Kalgoorlie and create a new supermarket for the people here you have my support," he said.

"Fundamentally, it's appalling that a group of faceless, anonymous people on the other side of Australia get involved in free enterprise here."

Landmark legal challenge

In July, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) exercised new powers to stop Coles from building a new supermarket and liquor store in the city, located about 600km east of Perth.

Among other factors in its decision, the watchdog cited the potential for Coles's expansion to knock out smaller independent competitors already operating in Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

Coles immediately appealed, in what looms as a test case for Australia's new merger laws.

There are six supermarkets in Kalgoorlie-Boulder, including an existing Coles in the CBD. (ABC News)

In one respect, the case was a David versus Goliath battle.

On one side was Coles, with 860 supermarkets nationwide, fighting to establish a second store in Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

The closest competitor, O'Connor Fresh IGA, is about 2km from the proposed new development and argued there is a "commercially real possibility" it would go out of business.

The closest competitor to the proposed Coles development is the O'Connor Fresh IGA. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Competitor flags market exit

ACCC lawyer Declan Roche SC insisted any Coles expansion represented a "substantial lessening of competition" across Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

He said the consumer watchdog assessed competition would be significantly impacted if O'Connor Fresh IGA exited the market, given its operating hours are not regulated like Coles and benefit local shift workers.

"The ACCC's view was it offers consumers a differentiated product in terms of range and service … and a measure of its effectiveness as a competitor is the proportion of Kalgoorlie grocery spend it attracts," Mr Roche told the tribunal.

"Coles' own business case … without getting into the confidential figures … identifies a proportion of Coles' business from the new supermarket will come from the business that's currently being done by O'Connor Fresh IGA."

The O'Connor Fresh IGA is the closest competitor to the site of the proposed Coles supermarket. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

With six existing supermarkets, Mr Roche described Kalgoorlie-Boulder as a "concentrated market" and backing the ACCC's position was the Kalgoorlie-Boulder Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

"The submission of the chamber of commerce is the expansion is neither necessary nor justified, wouldn't provide any meaningful increase in consumer choice and would over-saturate the market," he said.

O'Connor Fresh IGA's counsel Robert Yezerski SC told the tribunal the market had been impacted by last year's arrival of Tony Galati's Spudshed franchise in a "very material" way, which triggered a "competitive response" from national chains.

"We believe Coles takes more power we because it becomes less constrained by its competitors," he said.

WA businessman Tony Galati at the opening of Kalgoorlie-Boulder's Spudshed supermarket. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)

Future investment uncertain

But the supermarket giant argued the watchdog's intervention would have a "chilling effect" on investment in Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

The warning would be ominous for the City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder, which launched a nationwide marketing blitz in 2021 as part of its ambition to grow the population to 40,000 by the end of the decade.

"Any investor keen to expand its services in a market must weigh up the risk of an incumbent persuading the regulator, that its viability would be threatened if expansion were to occur," Coles's lawyer John Sheahan KC said.

"In many, perhaps most cases, the investor will be unable to make a confident or useful assessment of that risk.

"Given the transaction costs associated … that uncertainty will plausibly and likely have a chilling effect on proposed investments."

An aerial view of the Kalgoorlie CBD. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Coles previously operated two stores in Kalgoorlie-Boulder from 1986 to 2021.

Mr Sheahan argued consumers would get the benefits of Coles's national and state-based pricing structure, saying the proposed supermarket was "likely to intensify rather than diminish rivals' incentives to invest in dimensions of competition".

He noted Kalgoorlie-Boulder's growing population of fly-in, fly-out workers as a sign of increasing demand, while pointing to 10 regional locations across Australia with a comparable population.

"All have more supermarkets than Kalgoorlie, and nine of those towns have at least two Woolworths or two Coles," he said.

Case poses 'difficult dilemma'

The hearing delved deep into locals' purchasing habits, including Coles selling more dog food at its Kalgoorlie store than others across the country, while O'Connor Fresh IGA's biggest sellers included barbecue chickens and other takeaway offerings.

Mr Sheahan said Coles's biggest national competitor, Woolworths, is "unlikely to take the opening of a new Coles store lying down" and would likely pursue further investment or additional expansion.

It was also suggested another rival chain, Aldi, was weighing up entering the market.

The proposed site of the Coles supermarket in Somerville is currently bushland, which is surrounded by an industrial area, FIFO camp and childcare centre. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"All the consumers in Kalgoorlie are benefited by a new store," Mr Sheahan said.

"It is an odd reaction by the commission [ACCC] to say, 'Fine, just not too close to this store [O'Connor Fresh IGA], because it might make them uncomfortable.'"

Federal Court Justice Michael O'Bryan, the president of the tribunal's three-member panel, said the case posed a "difficult dilemma".

The property developer, M/Group, behind the proposed Amara Estate near Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport also plans to lease land to Coles for a new supermarket development. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"Some consumers may prefer the new supermarket because of location or lower prices or other features," Justice O'Bryan said.

" How do we judge that against the secondary consequences which may appear to be a reduction in competition? "

The tribunal has reserved its decision, and is required to make a final determination within 90 days.

title: 30,000-hectare carbon forestry project shoots up on remote island
text:
On the remote Tiwi Islands in the Northern Territory, a major carbon forestry project is taking shape.

More than 2 million Eucalyptus pellita seedlings have been planted on Melville Island this year across nearly 1,800 hectares, with some of those trees already 4 metres tall.

But this is just the start.

The overall project will see 30,000 hectares planted on the island, which will produce an estimated 12 million cubic metres of high-value wood products, as well as 5 million carbon credits over the life span of the project.

Tiwi Plantations chairman Gibson Farmer Illortaminni said he was excited about this new chapter for forestry on the Tiwis, referring to the seedlings as "his grandchildren".

"From the trees I planted in 1989, we collected seeds from them, so we can grow new trees for the second rotation," he said.

"We've got young Tiwi boys and girls here working on the seedlings and helping trees grow and it makes me proud because these young ones have jobs.

"There's not many jobs on the Tiwi Islands, but there's jobs here in forestry."

Planted as seedlings in early 2026, most of the Eucalyptus pellita trees are already 3 to 4 metres tall. (ABC Rural: Matt Brann)

The long journey to Eucalyptus pellita

The Tiwi Islands have a long and complicated history when it comes to forestry.

In the 1960s, the NT government started forestry trials on Melville Island.

Local sawmills were set up after Cyclone Tracy in 1974 to provide timber to help rebuild Darwin.

Then in the late 1990s, a decision was made by Tiwi people to clear land for plantation forestry.

In 2005, a company called Great Southern bought the project and invested heavily in the establishment of 30,000 hectares of Acacia mangium trees.

But like many other managed investment schemes at the time, Great Southern hit trouble, and fell into receivership in 2009.

Tiwi Islanders watch the first loading of woodchips at Port Melville in 2015. (ABC Rural: Daniel Fitzgerald)

The Tiwi people formed their own forestry company (Tiwi Plantations Corporation) to take over the project, and worked hard to get the trees through to harvest, eventually exporting more than 1 million tonnes of Acacia mangium woodchips.

But by their own admission, the Acacia mangium trees were not the commercial success many had hoped for.

At the start of this year, Tiwi Plantations finalised an $81 million investment with River Capital and the Clean Energy Finance Corporation to create a carbon forestry project, which will involve replanting the full 30,000 hectares with Eucalyptus pellita.

Flying over Melville Island you can see the land that has been prepared for tree planting. (ABC Rural: Matt Brann)

Multiple uses

Tiwi Plantations project manager Chris Oliver said Eucalyptus pellita had a number of benefits.

"Over the decades there's been various trials on the island, but Eucalyptus pellita has shone above the rest," he said.

"It's a good species that grows well in the conditions here, but not only does it have good growth rates, it has great potential for multiple products [once harvested]."

The Eucalyptus pellita's growth rate is much better than the Acacia mangium trees that were previously planted on the Tiwi Islands. (Supplied: Tiwi Plantations)

Mr Oliver said the University of Melbourne was researching the timber's potential for engineered wood products for the construction sector.

"We're not just looking to export everything to customers overseas," he said.

"We're also looking at local production on the island to utilise the resource and put some of this into local housing."

Mr Illortaminii said if some of the timber could be used locally it would be a great outcome.

"This Eucalyptus pellita is a really good wood and very strong," he said.

"They stand up strong in the wind compared to those Acacia mangiums."

Eucalyptus pellita seedlings in the nursery on Melville Island. (ABC Rural: Matt Brann)

Carbon credits 'a game changer'

The project on the Tiwi Islands is not only about timber, it is also understood to be Australia's largest First Nations-led carbon initiative.

Australian carbon credit units (ACCU) from the project are expected to become available from 2027, with the project expected to generate about 5 million ACCUs under the Plantation Forestry (schedule 1) methodology over its lifetime.

A generic ACCU is currently worth about $38, although Indigenous-led projects with co-benefits often attract a premium price.

Mr Oliver said having a revenue stream in the years before harvest was a "game changer" for forestry projects.

"One of the big things about forestry is it requires a lot of investment at the start and it takes a long time to make a return," he said.

"So this project has been developed to produce carbon credits, which helps us to become self-funding.

"Having that revenue stream coming in, in the early stage of the plantation, changes the game completely."

Jobs for Tiwis

The next round of planting is due to start in December, with about 3.8 million seedlings being prepared at the Yapilika Forestry Centre's nursery.

Darnelle Clayton has started a traineeship with the nursery and said she had been learning a lot.

"This is my first month as a trainee and so far I've learnt about planting, how they grow, and how they could be used in the future," she said.

"My mum works here and she kind of inspired me."

Darnelle Clayton is a trainee working at the Yapilika Forestry Centre. (ABC Rural: Matt Brann)

Ms Clayton said she was keen to become a leader at the nursery and inspire others.

She said it would be great to be involved with the project long enough to see the first harvest.

"I'm definitely excited for when [harvest arrives]; I want to see that moment for myself and will feel very proud knowing how much hard work went into it."

Tiwi workers represent about 60 per cent of the current workforce, earning more than $1.4 million in direct wages this year.

Mr Oliver said the island was very busy preparing about 3,800 hectares for planting in 2027.

"We're very buoyant about this project and I think it's going to be a talking point of the Tiwi Islands for the next 30 to 40 years," he said.

title: Ambulance volunteers left to fundraise $600,000 for new depot
text:
Ambulance volunteers across regional Western Australia are calling on the state government to increase funding, with many questioning why they are responsible for meeting the cost of new ambulances and infrastructure.

WA is one of two Australian jurisdictions, along with the Northern Territory, where St John Ambulance provides ambulance services under contract to the health department.

Volunteers play a critical role, particularly in smaller regional communities where sub-centres are volunteer-run.

Ivan Woodhams is the chair of St John Walpole, about 410 kilometres south of Perth, he said volunteers at the depot have fundraised more than $600,000 to replace its aging headquarters.

Similar stories can be found in sub-centres across the state.

"From here to Kununurra, every sub-centre is under the same expectation to provide everything that they use," Mr Woodhams said.

" The cost of an ambulance service is astronomical ... for the years and jobs that we do, we accumulate very little. "

Ivan Woodhams says the cost of an ambulance service is "astronomical". (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

About 20 people volunteer at the sub-centre which services communities around Walpole and Nornalup, both popular tourist destinations.

While efforts to get a new building off the ground have been substantial, Mr Woodhams said costs are rising quicker than they can keep up with.

"We've had significant local donations," he said.

"We're getting towards what we thought was going to be enough, but as the years have progressed, I fear that we'll be well short of the final figure."

He wants the state government to step in and subsidise the cost.

" We have to pay for it and take funds literally out of the hands of locals. "

Kath Broadbent has spent more than 30 years volunteering with the Walpole branch. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

A voice for volunteers

Further inland, Travis Hawkins has been a member of Gnowangerup's sub-centre for a decade.

He is part of a new advocacy group designed to bridge the gap between volunteers and St John's management.

It includes members from across regional WA hoping to identify a sustainable funding model for volunteer centres.

Gnowangerup St John's Travis Hawkins is part of a new group bridging the gap between country centres and St John WA. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

While patient transfer fees and other work within the community provide alternative income streams, Mr Hawkins said both volunteers and St John management recognised the need for change.

"The model we currently have is not fit for purpose anymore," he said.

"In some areas the income is not sufficient (to cover costs), while in other areas it's an abundance, that's why we have raised this inequity."

Mr Hawkins said more government support from any level would make funding the sub-centres easier.

Emergency equipment used in ambulances must be replaced every four to 10 years. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

A St John WA spokesperson said investment was prioritised by demand and workforce needs.

"We recognise that the ability of individual communities to fundraise varies, and essential safety and minimum-standard infrastructure should not depend on a community’s fundraising capacity," the spokesperson said.

An ambulance at the St John Walpole depot. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

"Local fundraising can, however, help support local priorities and additional investment.

"We continue to work with communities and government to ensure regional ambulance infrastructure is sustainable, fit for purpose and prioritised according to need."

The state government has been contacted for comment.

title: Dawn Fraser fired up for 1956 Melbourne Olympics reunion
text:
Amid the reunions and celebrations, Dawn Fraser is drawing some inspiration from the 70th anniversary of the Melbourne Olympics.

Australia's most famous Olympian has come to Melbourne for a lunch on Sunday at the MCG to mark the November 22 opening ceremony date of the 1956 Games.

Fraser is 89 and had to miss a commemorative 1956 Olympics dinner in Melbourne a few weeks ago because of a health issue.

Fraser says she will go from table to table in her wheelchair to meet old friends and make new ones at the lunch, which coincides with the opening ceremony at the MCG 70 years ago.

Asked if she might be there for the 2032 Brisbane Olympics — Fraser was also a key figure at the Sydney 2000 Games — there is a reminder of what made her an all-time sporting great.

TV memories of the 1956 Olympics Watching the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Games was many Australians' first experience of television.

"I would love to be there at '32, to support our athletes," Fraser told AAP.

"I think of my age — I just turned 89 — and, 'Oh well, that's so many years off.' But then when I look at some of the athletes who are coming to this testimonial, some of them are 95, 99.

"Then I'm thinking — excuse the expression — 'Shit! I can do that. If they can do it, I can do it.'"

Likewise, the 19-year-old from a hardscrabble Balmain upbringing had her eyes opened wide at the 1956 Olympics.

Until then, Fraser had only swum against other Australians.

"I never thought about it. [To me, the Olympics] was just another swimming event. But when I won my gold medal, I realised how big it was," Fraser said.

"It wasn't until after I won … competing against so many nations.

"To win a gold medal was something out of this world. You didn't think about it until a month later, that you were the best swimmer in the world."

Fraser won the 100-metre freestyle in Melbourne and was a member of the 4x100 women's freestyle relay team that also claimed gold.

Dawn Fraser (centre) began her Olympic reign in the 100m freestyle in Melbourne. She won her third straight gold in Tokyo in 1964. (Getty Images: Central Press/Hulton Archive)

She went on to become the first of only four swimmers who have won gold in the same individual event at three-successive Olympics. Somewhere in there, she became "Our Dawn".

Two days after the reunion, the Sport Australia Hall Of Fame annual dinner will feature the Dawn Award. It goes to an individual, team or organisation that shows courage, breaks new ground and changes sport for the better.

But as far as Fraser is concerned, she is just one athlete at the reunion.

"I'm an athlete among athletes, and I'm very proud to be among the athletes who I met and competed against in 1956," she said.

Just as the Melbourne Games dramatically changed Fraser's life, it also was a landmark for Australian sport. Only 11 years after World War Two, Australia was still an international backwater.

It has been 70 years today since Ron Clarke lit the Olympic cauldron at the MCG to kick off the Games in 1956. (Getty Images)

"Here we were, a small country, having an Olympic event that meant so much to a lot of sportsmen and women in our country … and throughout the world," Fraser said.

"We were holding the biggest sporting event ever in Olympic history.

"It was the start of not only my swimming career but for a lot of other sportsmen and women in Australia — the start of their international careers.

"It was a big stepping stone for all of us because we didn't realise we were competing against the best athletes in the world."

And so to 2032, where Fraser hopes Australia can raise the bar again.

"I want them to make it as successful as all the other Olympic Games — if not a little bit better. It's very hard to do that, but Sydney, I thought the same thing," she said.

"Sydney outshone Melbourne and I'm sure Brisbane will outshine Sydney."

All hope is not lost for players whose AFL dreams were not realised at the national draft. The rookie draft on Monday is the next chance for footballers to join, or rejoin, a list, while others – including a crop of delisted players – will need to train with a club across summer to audition for a pre-season supplementary selection period (SSP) spot. Collingwood’s Harry DeMattia, Saints Dan Butler and Ryan Byrnes, Western Bulldog Riley Garcia, the Brisbane Lions’ Luke Lloyd and Koby Evans, and Fremantle’s Jaren Carr all have promises to return to their club in the rookie draft. Switching places: Former top 10 pick Nik Cox is no longer at Essendon, but Bailey Banfield is set to arrive. AFL Photos There is less certainty, but still a flicker of hope for the likes of the Camporeale twins – Ben and Lucas – who will be fighting to reclaim a place on Carlton’s list under new coach Josh Fraser, while cut Bomber Nik Cox may train with Fremantle in pursuit of an SSP place.

Advertisement

Ex-Swan Harry Cunningham will sign a two-year deal with Adelaide after Sydney offered him only one to stay. The Blues can make up to three picks at the rookie draft. “We might just go with one and have some train-on players over the off-season,” Blues football boss Chris Davies said. “We think the balance of players that we’ve just brought in helps to balance the list ... they’re [the Camporeales] still players we’re going to think about. We’ll make that final decision after the rookie draft.” Essendon are expected to sign ex-Docker Bailey Banfield and former Kangaroo Tyler Sellers in the SSP, as well as key-position swingman Nathan Kreuger via the new First Nations category B list rule.

Advertisement

The AFL granted the Bombers two extra rookie-list spots in September as an assistance package, with league chief executive Andrew Dillon strongly hinting they needed to be used on experienced players. Related Article AFL 2026 More than 60 players were picked in the AFL draft. Here’s who your club selected, and what they said about it “We’ll have the weekend to consider our options, but we have one spot available in the rookie draft, and we’d like to bring in some more mature talent through our additional rookie spots as well,” Essendon list boss Matt Rosa said. The AFL introduced the First Nations rule to encourage clubs to sign Indigenous talent without list limitations. So far, clubs appear to mostly be using it to commit to former AFL players, such as Kreuger, James Bell (GWS), Liam Jones (Gold Coast) and Isaac Keeler (Port Adelaide), although the Western Bulldogs are looking at Footscray midfielder Cooper Craig-Peters, who made the VFL’s team of the year in 2026.

Advertisement

Suns list boss Kall Burns confirmed that Jones was a “player of interest”. Brisbane’s national recruiting manager Steve Conole confirmed that they never considered the ex-Bulldogs and Blues defender despite him being a development coach at the Lions this year. Another player tipped to be signed is Northern Knights defender Kai Parker, who is a Collingwood next-generation academy member. Parker suffered a season-ending shoulder injury, but impressed this year. Richmond NGA midfielder Tanner Armstrong, Northern Territory’s Sonny Smiler and South Fremantle forward Cam Maynard could also be in the mix. Three players who were All-Australians at this year’s AFL under-18 championships – interceptor Billy Wigmore, endurance king Albert Macgowan and sharpshooting tall forward Jack Slattery – did not find a club in the national draft.

Macgowan won the Sandringham Dragons’ best-and-fairest award and ran the two-kilometre time trial in less than six minutes at the draft combine, but there are concerns about his lack of speed. Others who received some pre-draft buzz but were overlooked included Gippsland Power’s Marlon Neocleous and Cody Templeton – who was adjudged the best player afield in the Talent League grand final – and Eastern Ranges forward Zac Antonellos. A spacious, double-storey Northcote apartment above a shop on bustling High Street sold for $945,000 in post-auction negotiations on Saturday, $5000 below its advertised reserve. With three bedrooms, two bathrooms and a large open-plan living, dining and kitchen area on its second level, 3/597 High Street is minutes’ walk from landmark Northcote venues The Croxton, The Thornbury Local and cocktail bar Kitty Somerset. The strip was named “the coolest street in the world” by Time Out magazine in 2024. The property was one of 770 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 52 per cent from 523 reported results throughout the week, while 105 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The clearance rate remains in the low 50s, and is likely to be revised down further when more results are reported. Agents say lower stock levels, rate hikes, state and federal legislative changes and the looming state election are all combining to hold buyers back from bidding.

Advertisement

The Northcote apartment had a listed reserve of $950,000, and given its location and stairs, was “very much a young person’s property”, Woodards Northcote-Thornbury lead agent Andrew Guarino said. “Obviously it’s pretty unique,” he said. “And free from any body corporate, which was a plus.” The city view from the apartment’s second-floor balcony was a definite selling point for the “young person’s property”. Woodards Northcote-Thornbury Auctioneer Mario Buttera opened the auction with an $850,000 vendor bid, and from there, two bidders – both first home buyers – traded quick $25,000 increments, slowing to $10,000, $5000 and eventually $1000 bids as the price cleared the $900,000 mark, and passed in at $935,000. The first round of post-auction negotiations failed, with the high bidders failing to secure the home. The underbidder, there with his father, then increased his offer and bought it.

Advertisement

“There was a bit of backwards and forwards, but it sold pretty much immediately,” Guarino said. The vendor was a long-term investor selling to consolidate his portfolio. In Elsternwick, a white weatherboard Victorian home sold for $1.21 million at auction, after briefly looking like it might pass in without a single bid. The semi-detached, picket-fenced house at 21 Downshire Road features the wider, more generous blocks that Woodards Elsternwick agent and auctioneer Sam Paynter said the suburb, and Downshire Road in particular, is “well known and well regarded” for.

Advertisement

With an advertised reserve of $1.15 million, Paynter said its 30-year-old renovation had attracted buyers because it had updated the property in “very much the same way you would do it now”. The rear paved courtyard and open-plan kitchen and entertaining area were key features for buyers. Woodards Elsternwick The house was sold as part of an estate, and had been repainted and recarpeted to “bring it up to speed” before sale. Paynter opened the auction by asking for a bid from the street and, after failing to attract one, paused briefly to check in with his vendors. He then returned to place a vendor bid of $1.1 million. “And off it went from there,” he said, with two bidders trading $10,000 and $5000 increments until the auction came to a close. A downsizing couple secured the home, narrowly beating a young local couple.

Advertisement

Despite the sale, the auctioneer thought federal tax changes, as well as the recent Victorian government requirement for reserves to be advertised at least seven days before auction, had “delivered total uncertainty to the market”, leading to buyer reluctance in the midst of a price correction. Related Article Auctions Stunning inner-east townhouse sells for $2.11 million “But I think once we get through this year, we should be on for a more positive first quarter next year,” he said. In Gladstone Park, a three-bedroom house on a 597-square-metre block sold for $738,000 under the hammer, after a long battle between three bidders. The home at 17 Vaucluse Avenue was renovated by the owner - a plumber - soon after he purchased it for his family for $315,000 in 2008.

Advertisement

Featuring polished timber floors, an updated bathroom and kitchen, and a rear deck and fire pit for entertaining, the property had an advertised reserve of $711,000. Ray White Sunbury agent and auctioneer Aaron Hill said a genuine $650,000 bid opened the auction, with the price jumping up in $10,000 increments until it reached $680,000. Bidding then slowed to $5000 increments before hitting $710,000. From there, 28 separate $1000 bids were traded between the three buyers until it sold. Hill said all three bidders were first home buyers, and a young local couple won. The vendors have moved further in to take advantage of school zoning.

Advertisement

While the local market was “fine”, Hill thought buyers were missing out on good properties – scared off by advertised reserves that were outside their budget, even as many homes were selling for less after auction. “It doesn’t matter what we say ... they just don’t bother turning up when they see the reserve,” he said. As a teenage schoolboy and social media phenomenon, Taniela Tupou made his name by scoring 50-metre tries. But the muscle memory had mostly faded when the 30-year-old Tupou found himself in the clear with a ten-metre run to the try line against Wales. Loading “Obviously we made a break, I ended up in the back line and I heard Tom Wright saying, ‘Run off me, run off me’,” Tupou said. “That’s all I did. I did not expect the ball, and he passed me the ball. I almost didn’t know what to do, with no one next to me. “It was probably the easiest try I’ve ever scored. I didn’t have to touch anyone.”

Advertisement

Will it end up as an 50-metre try when you tell the story to your grandkids? “I felt like it was 80 metres,” Tupou grinned. “I can’t remember the last time I scored, so it’s good to score one for the boys.” Taniela Tupou is mobbed by teammates after scoring the opening try. Getty Tupou’s first-half score, which saw him take a flat pass from Wright in the 22nd minute and helped Australia take an early lead, was one of several influential moments from the big prop that contributed to the Wallabies’ win. Tupou had been promoted to the starting front row with Isaac Kailea and Bradon Paenga-Amosa, and all three played strongly. Along with the try, Tupou’s breakdown work and stinging defence saw him wind back the clock, albeit with a few scrum penalties conceded too.

Advertisement

The win was huge for the Wallabies, said Tupou, after some challenging weeks of massive losses against New Zealand and England, and a tight one to Scotland. “It’s a bloody good feeling, mate. You know, what it’s like the last couple of weeks, it’s been tough for us,” Tupou said. Wallabies coach Les Kiss with Tom Wright and Kurtley Beale after the victory over Wales. Getty Images “Winning changes everything. You’re not sore after a game or after a win. A win just takes away the pain, really. It’s a good feeling, mate. It’s been a while since we’ve won, a couple of weeks, months since our last win. It’s good to get it up tonight, but the work starts now. Hopefully, we can pick it up next Friday.” The Wallabies will now play Ireland in the Nations Championship finals at Twickenham on Friday (Saturday morning, AEDT). They finished third in the Southern table, behind South Africa and New Zealand, who will play France and England in the gold and silver matches respectively.

Advertisement

The northern hemisphere grouping has been dominant in November, but Tupou insisted the Irish – who dominated the Springboks at the weekend – wouldn’t have it all their own way. Related Article Analysis

Australian rugby Wallabies player ratings: Suaalii returns to form as big names stand tall “We’ll be so up for this game,” Tupou said. “It is a big challenge coming up. They just beat the world champions, the South Africans. It’s not going to be easy. We’re going to be up for it. It’s going to be a good challenge for us. “Obviously we lost to England and just lost to Scotland. Today, it didn’t matter how we win – big win or small win, all we needed was just a win. It changes everything. You don’t forget about what happened in the last couple of weeks, but it just changes the mood. “You’re happy, like you want to do it again. When you lose, it’s just such a shit feeling. It takes a couple of days to get over it. By the time you recover, it’s bloody Thursday. A few days to get ready for the game.

Advertisement

“Hopefully, this will give us a bit of confidence going into the game against Ireland.” The strong performances of players promoted to the starting team in Wales will give Kiss plenty of food for thought for this week’s clash. Tupou said he genuinely didn’t care if he starts or comes off the bench. “It doesn’t bother me – whatever Les thinks is best for the team against Ireland,” Tupou said. “If it’s early in my career, I would 100 per cent want to play. But now I’m just, ‘Whatever’s best for the team’.

A local couple paid $8.58 million for a grand Kirribilli home at auction on Saturday, bidding over the phone from Madrid. The five-bedroom house at 60 Willoughby Street dates to the 1880s but has been refurbished with sympathetic updates, a Caesarstone kitchen, outdoor dining area and an upstairs bedroom with a soaring ceiling. The property was one of 984 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 47 per cent from 560 reported results throughout the week, while 225 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The result is a modest increase on last week’s early read of 45 per cent, the equal lowest preliminary result this year, but remains well below the threshold of 60 per cent that indicates a market balanced between buyers and sellers.

Advertisement

The Kirribilli home, known in the area as “the blue house”, had a price guide of $8.5 million and attracted two bidders at auction. Related Article Auctions ‘Quality home’: Paddington terrace sells for $310,000 above reserve Bidding began at $8.35 million and rose fast at first. Proceedings slowed once the price reached $8.5 million, which was also the reserve price, and from there the parties traded $10,000 bids, The Agency selling agent Sandro Petrini said. The winners are a local owner-occupier couple who used to live nearby and missed living there, he said. “It is one of those unique houses, everyone calls it ‘the blue house’, everyone loves it that lives there locally.”

Advertisement

He said the winning bidders were in Madrid, where it was the middle of the night, and bidding by phone. The underbidders were from the lower north shore. He thought if the market was stronger there might have been another two, three or four bidders for the home. “It is just a unique home,” Petrini said. “It is private because it is a diamond-shaped block.” He said the home was in great condition, noting the cornices, ceilings and three-car garage. “The formal part of it is sensational and then you have got the more modern part as well.”

Advertisement

Asked about the market in general, he described conditions as “terrible”, then reflected. “It is not terrible, it is just, the buyers are very nervous, that is all,” he said. “This is the best time to be buying.” In Strathfield, a contemporary architect-designed home sold for $9.6 million after four parties registered and all four of them bid. The five-bedroom home at 61 Cotswold Road featured natural stone, a butler’s pantry, a swimming pool and outdoor dining area. The first bid was $8.7 million and the price rose in increments of $100,000 to start, then $50,000.

Advertisement

The home sold under the hammer for its reserve price of $9.6 million, which was also the price guide, to a local family who are upsizing. The vendors are also upsizing to a bigger block in the same suburb. Related Article Title Deeds Rock star sells Point Piper apartment after years-long campaign McGrath Strathfield selling agent Tarun Sethi thought the home stood out for its construction quality and its location in the “Golden Mile” of Strathfield. He thought the market broadly was performing well, noting his team has sold $41 million of Strathfield real estate in the last four days. “The market seems to be fairly strong in Strathfield still, despite a lot of the noise,” he said.

“Around the market, people are realising that if they don’t buy now, they might catch themselves buying in the upswing in the next year.” He noted the rise in unemployment in the latest jobs data, which he thought made it unlikely there would be further interest rate hikes. In Concord, a man paid $1.68 million for a fixer-upper that also had the potential to become a site for a new dream home. The three-bedroom house at 4 Spring Street had a price guide of $1.7 million and attracted five registered bidders, of whom four were active.

Black Friday bargain hunters have been urged to stay alert for counterfeit shopfronts and AI-generated content as the national scams agency observes a global rise in deepfake content. Cybersecurity experts and consumer protection agencies have warned against lookalike websites masquerading as legitimate brands spruiking too-good-to-be-true deals, as the nation is forecast to spend a record $7.2 billion in the four days between Black Friday on November 27 and Cyber Monday on the 30th. Black Friday is one of the biggest shopping events of the year. AP The National Anti-Scam Centre (NASC), a consumer protection body that sits within the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, said law enforcement partners, regulators and global counterparts had all observed a global rise in artificial intelligence tools being exploited to create highly realistic, personalised websites, particularly in online shopping and investment. “The National Anti-Scam Centre has observed more concerns and reports this year about AI-cloned storefronts, deepfake brand or celebrity ads, and ‘news’ items,” a spokesperson said in a statement to this masthead.

Advertisement

More than one in two (58.7 per cent) of all Scamwatch reports in the first nine months of this year were buying and selling scams. More than 11,500 victims lost $17.2 million during this period, according to NASC figures. Related Article Black Friday 16 of the best Christmas gifts to shop on Amazon during the Black Friday sales Common scams can include shops claiming to go out of business and giving away items free of charge, or websites that have poorer-quality images or incomplete information. Shoppers should be wary of websites that appear to have AI-generated images or video or missing basic business or contact information. Check the retailer’s official website instead of responding to unsolicited messages or links in texts or emails. “Fake shops and fake sales are among the biggest issues, and they invariably increase just before major holidays,” said Bitdefender cybersecurity specialist Silviu Stahie. “A fairly typical example in Australia is ads for shops that are going out of business and clearing their stock, with items given away free of charge.” Scammers will be attempting to capitalise on a false sense of urgency and FOMO (fear of missing out), which are already heightened in a sales environment.

Advertisement

“Black Friday is particularly ripe for this because shoppers are expecting to be bombarded with ads, flash deals and messages telling them to act quickly,” said ING head of consumer insights Matt Bowen. Popular games with a global cult following like Grand Theft Auto VI can make victims of those who fall for offers that look convincing. Malicious actors have been caught selling PC versions of the game, which doesn’t exist. “Scammers are very good at following the hype,” added Bowen. “If you suddenly see offers for exclusive access, heavily discounted copies, downloads or giveaways, particularly through an unexpected ad or link, it’s worth taking a moment to check that it’s legitimate and going directly to the official retailer.” Well-known retailers offering deep discounts of 50 to 90 per cent off should be viewed with some wariness, as should congratulatory messages claiming the consumer has won a reward or prize. “If something seems too good to be true, it probably is,” said digital safety software platform TrendLife head of consumer education Lynette Owens. “And if an offer is too tempting to turn down, always check the brand’s official pages and channels to confirm if the deal is real.”

Advertisement

Courier and postal service scams are always rife at this time of year, with Australia Post, FedEx and DHL frequently impersonated from Black Friday throughout the holiday season, she warned. “It’s the busiest time of the year for deliveries, and cyber criminals are watching for any chance to exploit your eagerness to receive your parcels.” Related Article Black Friday Watchdog warns retailers over fake Black Friday deals and false urgency The ACCC is watching Shoppers have learned to expect deals and markdowns well before Black Friday, which typically falls on the last Friday of November. On average, Australian retailers are kicking off Black Friday sales about two weeks earlier, with delivery platform Shippit seeing 10 per cent more online orders than the same period last year. The consumer watchdog has warned retailers against misleading practices, including “sitewide” or “storewide” claims that actually exclude several products, time-limited offers, false claims about remaining stock that pressure shoppers into purchasing, and was/now prices in which those items were never or not recently sold at those prices.

The ACCC’s 2025 Black Friday sweep of 50 retailers saw James Lane and Vuly penalised nearly $60,000 for creating a false sense of urgency, while Booktopia owner digiDirect paid $99,000 for misleading was/now claims. This year, the maximum corporate penalty for retailers falling foul of Australian consumer law has doubled from $50 million to $100 million per contravention. “Retailers need to be careful about creating a false sense of urgency with claims such as ‘ends today’, ‘last chance’ or countdown timers, particularly if the same discounts continue or the sale is extended,” said law firm Holding Redlich special counsel Emily Booth. “There is also a risk that a ‘sale’ price effectively becomes the standard price.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
