title: This is a tale that many may not know well, but its consequences are still felt today
text:
Advertisement

Key points OPERA: Opera Australia bring Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan to Melbourne

JAZZ: The Vampires perform at Bennetts Lane Jazz Club

MUSIC: ACO finishes the season on a high note with Beethoven’s Pastoral

THEATRE: Novel, movie and now a play: A Room With A View comes to MTC

MUSIC: Aldous Harding performs to a sold out crowd at Forum Melbourne

OPERA

Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan ★★★

Playhouse, Arts Centre Melbourne, until November 28 A man is suspended in mid-air above a body of water that stretches across the stage. He descends, drowning as he falls. It’s a visceral opening, the ensuing tale one that Australians may not know well, but the consequences of which are still felt today. Sebastian Geilings is gut-wrenchingly stunning in Opera Australia’s Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan. Ben Fon Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan first premiered at the Adelaide Festival in 2022. It is a work by Brisbane composer Joseph Twist and librettists Alana Valentine and Christos Tsiolkas, the production devised by Neil Armfield. Opera Australia now brings Watershed to the Arts Centre. We begin with the 1972 death of Dr George Duncan, who drowned in Adelaide’s River Torrens. Herein lies the “watershed”. It’s this tragic event that leads to the decriminalisation of homosexual acts in South Australia. We agonisingly watch as three police officers are tried and acquitted in relation to Dr Duncan’s death.

Advertisement

The crime remains unsolved. The subject matter is deeply serious and is intended to be confronting. Anyone familiar with Tsiolkas – known for his colloquialisms and liberal use of profanity – might have known what was coming. Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan Ben Fon Coupled with the experience of Valentine, a doyenne of verbatim theatre (where transcripts of real people are taken and morphed into, usually, a play), the libretto is plainly, astonishingly blue. Which is certainly what 1970s Adelaideans would have sounded like, but when language is so naturalistic yet sung operatically (the most unnaturalistic), an unintended side effect that can sneak in is caricature. At times, this plot, involving a real person’s life lost in devastating circumstances, felt trivialised.

Advertisement

Joseph Twist is known to those of us with young children as a composer on Bluey, but his music crosses all boundaries. With influences of Bach, Sondheim, Pink Floyd and others, this score feels closer to musical theatre than oratorio, as it is referred to in the program. What it isn’t, is opera. Whether anyone cares about that is in the eye of the beholder. Musical theatre tenor Blake Appelqvist takes on the main role of the Lost Boy, and does so with deft sweetness, though their voice lacks resonance. Geilings with Blake Appelqvist as Lost Boy. Ben Fon The chorus are the real stars; Twist gives them layers upon layers of harmonies, with various moments for individual choristers to shine. Sebastian Geilings, the aforementioned dangling dancer, is gut-wrenchingly stunning. Though the period-ambiguous costumes did not aid the storytelling, Armfield’s direction is clever and undoubtedly powerful. After more than 50 years, this story deserves the spotlight, and many will be moved by it, no matter the manner in which it is told.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

JAZZ

The Vampires ★★★★

Bennetts Lane Jazz Club, November 21 At a time when the Australian music industry is facing multiple challenges – rising costs, insecure conditions and the existential threat of AI – it’s heartening to see a queue snaking down the street outside a local jazz club. The Vampires are a band whose warmth is key to their sonic signature. It’s even more heartening to see a new venue open when so many are closing, and to see it filled to the rafters for a concert by a long-running Australian jazz quartet. Sydney band The Vampires tour here regularly, but this was their first show in The JazzLab’s newly unveiled second room (named Bennetts Lane after owner Michael Tortoni’s previous club in the CBD), with excellent acoustics and twice the capacity of JazzLab.

Advertisement

Those acoustics served the band well on Saturday night at the Melbourne launch of their latest album, Skydancer. On the recording, all four players added extra layers and electronic effects in post-production. On stage, they layered and processed the sound in real time, enhancing the music’s textural depth without ever smothering its warmth. Related Article Melbourne live reviews My Fair Lady has arrived, and it’s an abso-bloomin’-lutely loverly treat That’s crucial for a band whose warmth is key to its sonic signature, along with memorable twin-horn themes and loping, dub-inflected grooves. Saxophonist Jeremy Rose and trumpeter Nick Garbett both used pedals to add reverb and delay to their instruments, but it was the creativity of their interactions – dancing in relaxed unison or taut harmonic lines, and engaging in energetic, improvised conversations – that made the music feel alive. Noel Mason could alter the tone of his electric bass at will (fat and insistent, or light and guitaristic), but could also switch to acoustic bass for a brighter, breezier sound. And while drummer Alex Masso added an occasional touch of reverb to his snare, it was the invention of his touch that provided the music’s rhythmic vitality, via languid backbeats, polyrhythmic shuffles or a swift, heady propulsion. Now in their 21st year, The Vampires are still finding new ways to expand their creative vision, without losing sight of the approachability – and humanity – that makes their music so appealing.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas

Advertisement

MUSIC

Beethoven’s Pastoral ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, November 21 It was a triple treat in more ways than one. For its final national tour of the year, the Australian Chamber Orchestra served up a winning trifecta of contrasting Beethoven works: the Coriolan Overture, the “Triple Concerto” and the “Pastoral” Symphony. Beethoven’s Pastoral was an uplifting end to another fruitful ACO season. Nic Walker Another treat was hearing the trio of lead violinist Richard Tognetti, principal cellist Timo-Veikko Valve and pianist Konstantin Shamray perform together as soloists in the unjustly neglected concerto. Forming a seamless prelude to the concerto’s quiet opening was the high drama of the Coriolan Overture. Thrumming with energy, the music was initially discharged in high-voltage chords before Tognetti ensured ongoing phrasing was flexible and well shaped.

Advertisement

There could have been no better way to celebrate Valve’s 20 years with the ACO than to collaborate with his friends in Beethoven’s charming amalgam of chamber and concerto styles. In all three movements, the cello has a starring role introducing the solo material and the golden, honeyed tone Valve’s Amati instrument made for unalloyed listening pleasure. Shamray’s use of a modern concert grand made perfect sense against an augmented ACO. Joined with Tognetti’s brighter-toned Guarneri del Gesù and period wind and brass, the entire ensemble filled Elisabeth Murdoch Hall with an impressive heft, warmth and clarity that could only be totally appreciated in person. Full of inventive detours, the concerto’s concluding Rondo alla Polacca made for an ebullient finale. Tognetti and his players gave a distinctly evocative account of Beethoven’s idyllic symphony; the period wind and brass giving the familiar music added piquancy. Ernst Schlader’s clarinet was a constant joy while the valveless horns were almost always stirring. Beethoven’s many contrasts were well pointed, not least the transition from the rustic country dancing into the ensuing thunderstorm and the eventual thanksgiving of the shepherds. What an uplifting end to another fruitful ACO season.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

THEATRE

A Room with a View ★★★

Melbourne Theatre Company, Southbank Theatre, until December 19 The first question the trepidatious theatregoer who has read E.M. Forster’s 1908 novel and seen the 1985 Merchant Ivory movie adaptation will ask is: do we even need a stage version? Nathalie Morris and Luke Wiltshire in A Room with a View. Brett Boardman It’s certainly treacherous territory to approach a much-loved classic with the aim of revitalising it for a new audience, and this iteration is an uneven one – not quite a tribute to the original text nor a wholesale modernisation. Adapted by Grace Chapple and directed by Hannah Goodwin, A Room with a View follows the convoluted getting-of-wisdom path of Lucy Honeychurch (Nathalie Morris) as she travels from England to Italy with her companion-chaperone cousin Charlotte (Hayley McElhinney).

Advertisement

Charlotte’s minder role seems to be a proprietary and protective one: to be in charge of Lucy’s moral education. After all, the Edwardian era dictates that a young, wealthy, unmarried woman of a certain class must conduct herself with decorum – which certainly does not extend to fraternising with men of questionable, socialist backgrounds. When Lucy meets and finds herself attracted to George Emerson (Luke Wiltshire) in Florence, she slowly begins to unbutton herself to possibilities beyond those predetermined for her. In terms of social standing, and despite his pomposity, Cecil Vyse (Charles Wu), a family friend, is a far more appropriate partner, but George offers a sense of the unknown, of freedom. Luke Wiltshire as George Emerson. Brett Boardman Wu brings an energy to him that’s not present in Wiltshire until the later scenes; so too does Tomáš Kantor, who doubles as Lucy’s exuberant brother Freddy and as an Italian driver. The rest of the cast acquit themselves well, including McElhinney’s turn as the shrewish, gossipy Charlotte and Tom Conroy as the vicar with secrets of his own. Chapple’s script moves from first-person dialogue to third-person narration, giving us both the individual and the omniscient perspective. Lucy’s sexual awakening is gradual and mired in confusion and self-deception.

Advertisement

Morris offers a spirited, open-eyed performance as she experiences the frisson of the new. But Wiltshire’s performance feels lacklustre next to her. Their budding relationship never feels genuinely lit up, and part of the problem lies with the disappointing, sparse set, which is primarily made up of a series of window frames upon which various scenes are projected – none memorable. The novel and the film both credit the glamour and radiance of Italy as pivotal to Lucy’s ripening – her falling into the throes of romance, but here such golden-lit vistas are missing. The set of A Room with a View is sparse. Brett Boardman There are no costuming updates; the production sticks to Edwardian period-appropriate clothing. However, there are some innovations to this adaptation that playfully lend themselves to theatricality, with various set pieces (a tennis match and the infamous lakeside skinny-dipping) that are wordless but dynamic and fun. While there are times when the momentum flags and it feels like there’s too much unnecessary exposition on the choices laid out for Lucy, one of the most poignant scenes is right towards the end, when McElhinney has her back to the audience and is looking out a window, her arms raised, leading us to wonder: will Charlotte ever have a possibility of choice like Lucy, a view of her choosing?

Reviewed by Thuy On

Advertisement

MUSIC

Aldous Harding ★★★★

Forum Melbourne, November 18 Tonight, New Zealand-born folk-pop songwriter Aldous Harding and her band spend most of the show sitting, meaning a lot of my view is the backs of people’s heads. If I angle it right, and the ocean of people sways in the right direction, I can see her, acoustic guitar in hand. But now what? Aldous Harding performs at the Forum. Richard Clifford Seeing her isn’t important tonight, and neither is small talk. Harding is no showboat. Between songs, she and the band mill silently, changing instruments, tuning. The audience wait patiently. The music converges somewhere over our heads. There’s plenty to fill the void left in place of sight lines and audience chatter. Harding’s songs are oblique. Much of tonight’s set is from her new album, Train on the Island.

Advertisement

Its songs are strange little machines, full of memorable images and unpredictable structures. She offers them with no context. “Mummy said my inception was like eating a pearl,” she sings on title track Train on the Island, over piano like knots in silk. Several tracks spin off into tangential outros, like on tonight’s highlight, If Lady Does It. The lyrics might be very personal, but she keeps herself at a tantalising distance. “This one’s about me,” she says in the introduction to Coats, but the chorus goes “Big thick coats on the dogs of people just trying to help.” Happily, we learn nothing tangible. Aldous Harding’s lyrics might be very personal, but she keeps herself at a tantalising distance. Richard Clifford “What is that accent?” my friend says during Leathery Whip. It’s no accent. It coils around Kiwi, American and something Germanic. These songs are from her subconscious, and she speaks her own language there. The sold-out crowd is mostly reverent, but silence invites people to fill it. A man yelps something incomprehensible. “So funny,” Harding almost whispers, dismissively. One fan yells out a too-complicated, impassioned plea that the lighting balance is wrong. “I can’t hear you, mate,” says Harding, and launches into Worms (“I flew down to the brewery / All wool dead on my waist”).

Advertisement

“You’ll be all right,” she says later. “I know the quiet is hard.” Related Article Visual art This artist wants you to leave her exhibition feeling odd – and ‘squished’ Harding closes her set with an encore of some older songs, Imagining My Man, with its twee little “Hey!” yelp, and the uncharacteristically sunny Designer (“Do not lose your young eyes / Laughing at good work with your ugly son”). As we leave, I hear a few people saying it would have been a perfect show if she played The Barrel, and if they could have seen her. I say embrace the obscured vision. There’s irreplicable joy in standing in silence with this many people, trying to get a glimpse at something you’ll never quite see and never quite understand.

Reviewed by Will Cox

Advertisement

MUSIC

Anne Sofie von Otter and Kristian Bezuidenhout ★★★★

Classical Music Australia, Melbourne Recital Centre, November 18 Swedish mezzo-soprano Anne Sofie von Otter has returned to Melbourne with the world-class stagecraft that has characterised her stellar career. Swedish mezzo-soprano Anne Sofie von Otter Presenting 16 Schubert songs with pianist Kristian Bezuidenhout, von Otter impressed an appreciative audience by bringing her compelling storytelling skills to the composer’s unique world where happiness and sadness, hope and disappointment are codependent. Schubert’s famous trout featured early on, along with revelling impish spirits in The Ghost Dance.

Advertisement

Further evidence of von Otter’s chameleonic versatility came with a gentle Lullaby, D. 867, the lyrical solemnity of Mignon’s Let Me Appear So, D. 877 and the effective use of her rich lower register in the nocturnal rustlings of In the Forest, D. 708. Related Article Melbourne live reviews Jason Donovan makes Ken Kesey’s iconic ‘bull goose loony’ his own Bezuidenhout’s solo interludes included an engrossing account of Mozart’s bittersweet Rondo in A minor, K. 511, very aligned with the Schubertian mood, while later came a spiky reading of Schubert’s Hungarian Melody in B minor, D. 817 and the long melodic arcs of the second-movement allegretto from the Piano Sonata in A minor, D. 537. In a lighter vein, four varied songs by von Otter’s 19th-century compatriot Adolf Lindblad proved a good foil for the final bracket of seven songs from Schwanengesang, D. 957, in which von Otter laid bare the stark anguish of unrequited love. Among Schubert’s last utterances, these songs include the popular Ständchen and Abschied, in which von Otter put on the lover’s brave face, while with Die Stadt and Der Doppelgänger came a confronting rawness.

Advertisement

Supported by Bezuidenhout’s empathy and dexterity, von Otter’s highly developed musicianship kept the focus on musical communication rather than on any understandable mellowing of her famously lustrous instrument. Two poignant encores, Schubert’s Lachen und Weinen and the ’60s hit Try to Remember, summed up the mood created by a memorable encounter with a great singer.

title: Las Vegas F1 GP LIVE: Piastri’s masterful drive from 17th to the podium as Verstappen shines in Vegas
text:
In the middle of the nail-biting Las Vegas Grand Prix, Oscar Piastri’s race was looking entirely mediocre, and borderline bleak.

The Australian driver had started in 17th place (after a grid penalty during qualifying) and had fought his way up the grid.

But multiple crashes and yellow flags bunched the drivers from nose-to-tail on track, leaving Piastri marooned in 11th.

The design and nature of the Las Vegas circuit led to some of the closest, nail-biting racing of 2026. Getty Images

He and Lando Norris were, as McLaren CEO Zak Brown plainly put it, “sitting ducks”.

Then everything changed.

After the restart Piastri executed sensational moves on Pierre Gasly and both Ferraris, storming away to fifth place. Next, he overtook Kimi Antonelli, but couldn’t match the Mercedes pace and dropped back.

McLaren issued Piastri a warning, reminding him that although he was doing a “great job” he needed to be “careful around his teammate”, Lando Norris, who was ahead of him.

Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris John Locher/Pool AP via AP

“Stop f-—ing telling me to be careful,” he said over the radio.

Undeterred, Piastri stayed close to the pack, waiting for the right moment.

Then it arrived.

With four laps to go, Piastri pounced on his teammate near Turn 5 snatching fourth place.

Then after fighting Max Verstappen and teammate Kimi Antonelli for the lead for nearly 47 laps, Russell locked up and went into the barriers.

Piastri found himself in third, but quickly lost his podium position to Norris who pounced.

But then Antonelli – who claimed the championship – faltered, and Piastri and Norris both swooped, claiming third and second respectively.

Nearly six and a half months since he last podium in Miami, Oscar Piastri’s drought was over.

As fireworks exploded over Sin City, Piastri beamed and looked lost for words.

Loading

“They say Las Vegas is the entertainment capital of the world, and I think that was pretty entertaining,” he said.

“Obviously starting from the back, I didn’t know how it was going to go… I could kind of work out pretty early on that it was just staying as one massive pack.”

The Las Vegas Grand Prix had 35 lead changes across 50 laps. It was as Lando Norris aptly put, “the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1”.

It’s a spectacular achievement for Piastri who has struggled with poor luck, performance and pace in 2026, crashing out of his home grand prix in Melbourne and suffering several DNF’s.

A podium is preciously what the Australian needed heading into the off-season.

It was carnage and devastation for George Russell who battled for the race win all day, only to come up short with two laps to go.

“This sort of race it was high-risk and high reward.… the lock-up, it was unavoidable, obviously disappointing, but I don’t regret it,” Russell said in a post-race interview.

The only drivers having a worse day were Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

The duo have bristled over the last few months, with Ferrari failing to implement strict rules on inter-team racing.

Tensions boiled over during the Las Vegas Grand Prix with Hamilton fumed over the radio, saying “Charles is just… Can you tell him to back the f--- off,”

Later in the race, the duo collided, with Hamilton spinning off track.l Leclerc later received a 10 second-time penalty for causing the collision.

The 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix will probably go down in history as the race that had it all; teammate skirmishes, crashes, and miraculous podium positions.

Key points MUSICAL THEATRE: My Fair Lady arrives at Arts Centre Melbourne

DANCE: [gameboy] at Dancehouse is a delightfully twisted dance satire

MUSIC: Opera Australia brings The Trumpet of the Swan to Regent Theatre

MUSIC: Foo Fighters put on three hours of rock’n’roll at Marvel Stadium

MUSICAL THEATRE

My Fair Lady ★★★★

Ian Potter State Theatre, until January 17 It’s been 70 years since My Fair Lady made its Broadway debut, and now it’s also opening in the brand-new, refurbished Ian Potter State Theatre. There’s a nice poetic twist to this production, as it’s based on the 2016 version, where Julie Andrews was at the directorial helm. Reg Livermore (centre) and the cast of My Fair Lady. Joe Armao Andrews was the original Eliza Doolittle, the impoverished Cockney flower girl who, with linguistic training, a new wardrobe and some etiquette lessons, was transformed into an aristocrat, fashionably fit to be presented to society. It’s a musical about the shape-changing potential of language, class and deportment in terms of social climbing – but most importantly, of realising your own self-worth. In this revival, director Karen Johnson Mortimer works with Andrews’ original staging. Based on George Bernard Shaw’s 1912 play, Pygmalion, the story has always been misogynistic and offensive when you strip it down to its bones: a young woman becomes a pawn, a game between two men who argue about whether she could be elevated by manipulating her speech and elocution and then presenting her for public approval as though she were a project they were tinkering with simply to amuse themselves.

Advertisement

The gender politics may be dated, but there’s no argument against the entertainment factor of gutter-to-ball transformation, nor the enduring quality of some of the songs in My Fair Lady. Judging by the reception on opening night, most of the audience knew all the lyrics to I Could Have Danced All Night, The Rain in Spain, On the Street Where You Live and Get Me to the Church on Time. Visually, it’s an abso-bloomin’-lutely loverly treat. This is a big, non-stinting, lavish production with live orchestra accompaniment; the costume design (particularly in the black-and-white Ascot event) is as gorgeous as you’d expect, and the sets, with their painted backdrops and architectural rendering, are detailed and sumptuous, from the bustling street scenes of Covent Garden to the chandeliered Embassy ballroom. Claire Lyon makes a feisty Eliza Doolittle. Joe Armao Claire Lyon makes a feisty Eliza; her metamorphosis from scrappy ingenue to someone wiser and jaded is seeded in emotional growth. Beneath the winsome charm, there’s a steeliness to her that Lyon manages to coax out. She realises that societal acceptance and social mobility are more complicated than just the ability to round your vowels and wear a fabulous frock. Colonel Pickering (Tony Llewellyn-Jones) and Henry Higgins, Professor of Phonetics (Nathaniel Parker), are both suitably pompous and avuncular; the bantering between them is easy and affectionate.

Advertisement

Parker has the difficult role of playing a charismatic bully but manages to negotiate the balance. Eliza’s father, Alfred (Reg Livermore), is an energetic livewire whose physicality belies his age, and Freddy Hellier as Eliza’s suitor is peppy and sweet. As Mrs Higgins, Robyn Nevin’s performance imperiously and wittily counterbalances the behaviour of her abrasive son, and Anne Wood as the housekeeper, imbues a commanding presence. The Ascot scene in particular is a visual highlight. Joe Armao Though this production is a homage to the original, the ending may be problematic for a modern audience hoping for a feminist reworking, as it leans toward the familiar tropes of reconciliation, romance and capitulation, rather than self-possession and emancipation – as conceived by Shaw who fought against a happy-ending pairing between the professor and his student. But regardless of its sexist undertones, My Fair Lady is musical theatre gold, and decades later, its lustre still shines brightly. Eliza’s real education is not on learning how to speak, but how to be heard.

DANCE

[gameboy] ★★★★

Dancehouse, until November 21 With its ritual humiliations and painful stunts, this delightfully twisted dance satire by choreographer Amy Zhang revels in the pointless masochism of so many viral internet videos. Funny but disturbing, it’s a work possessed by thoroughly unwholesome desires and impulses. [gameboy] by Amy Zhang Daniel Boud The show opens with a quote from American singer-songwriter Raveena: “The internet is like eating plastic.” It’s a complaint that could be read as a gloss for the whole performance. Online obsessions can fill up a life while offering little nourishment to the spirit. Zhang gives that appetite for empty stimulation a painfully physical form.

Advertisement

In the show’s longest section, she has her two dancers –Billy Keohavong and Ko Yamada – compete in a game show parody. Tasks include walking barefoot over Lego and transporting apples without hands. The loser of each round must brush their teeth with wasabi paste. In skimpy black briefs – one with a motorcycle helmet, the other in goggles – they maintain an affectless formality while completing their set tasks. The dancers maintain an affectless formality while completing their set tasks. Daniel Boud Winning and losing barely register. Only suppressed grunts during the penalty reveal the human agent beneath this ridiculous ceremony. The other sections are more dancerly but just as absurd. In one extended duet, unison gradually becomes bodily fusion. Rolling together across the stage, their tangled limbs resolve into a creature with four crablike legs, scuttling across the stage with disconcerting agility.

Advertisement

The final section recreates the candied choreography of K-pop group Girls’ Generation’s 2009 hit Gee. Keohavong and Yamada perform it with impressive lightness and zip, their energy apparently undiminished by the punishing ordeal they have just endured. Editor's pick Visual art This artist wants you to leave her exhibition feeling odd – and ‘squished’ It’s a weirdly comforting note on which to end. Two well-built, barely clothed men performing such a saccharine routine is funny, but there is a kind of wistful nostalgia in this moment of looking back. A longing for what the internet was or perhaps might have become. This show completes the Orbit program at Dancehouse, which introduced a series of work from interstate. Its slickness and nearly naked physicality feel distinctly Sydney: a welcome encounter with another city’s dance culture – and a persuasive argument for more interstate touring.

The Trumpet of the Swan ★★★

Opera Australia, Regent Theatre, until November 22 What business does an opera company have in staging a show that is without any singing at all? It’s a valid question, though Jason Robert Brown’s “novel symphony for actors and orchestra” is certainly not undeserving of a performance by Opera Australia. Arjun Tiwari as Louis in Opera Australia’s The Trumpet of the Swan. Ben Fon Based on the 1970 book by E.B. White (author of Charlotte’s Web and Stuart Little), the plot follows a young trumpeter swan born without a voice, who is given a literal trumpet and, of course, his uniqueness becomes his greatest strength. It is a coming-of-age story, really. Best known as a Broadway composer (The Last Five Years, Songs for a New World), Jason Robert Brown’s music is highly accessible and melodic without ever being basic. Sydney-based conductor Chad Kelly does a superb job of guiding Orchestra Victoria through the many compositional styles, with a lightness and ease that exudes appropriate playfulness. OV principal trumpet Mark Fitzpatrick is the star of the night, his solos sonorous and charming.

Following his highly acclaimed production of Grey Gardens, director Tyran Parke brings to the national opera company an outstanding troupe of Australian stage and small screen talent. Ben Mingay, from whom charisma overfloweth, is delightfully boisterous as Father Swan; Bert LaBonté an affable guide as the Storyteller, while Marney McQueen and Grant Piro both dazzle with an array of humorous accents and physical comedy. As the mute swan, dancer Arjun Tiwari moves with nimble elegance. Arhun Tiwari as Louis and Ben Mingay as Father Swan Ben Fon It is a tricky thing to mount, children’s entertainment with classical-ish orchestra; the closest thing to Trumpet in the standard repertory is Prokofiev’s well-known and beloved Peter and the Wolf. But if this show is truly intended for kids, perhaps a longer rehearsal period to allow for the actors to be off-book, plus colourful costumes and lively puppetry would allow for this production to, for want of a better word, sing.

Foo Fighters | Take Cover Tour ★★★★

Marvel Stadium, November 14 Welcome to Foo Fest 2026. Circle the belly of Marvel Stadium where bars, carnival-style cuisine and a robust smokers’ section swarm with Foo Fighters’ multigenerational fanbase. As the band takes the stage, charismatic master of dad rock Dave Grohl promises, firmly, to kick our asses with three hours of rock’n’roll. Dave Grohl is an impeccable frontman. Richard Clifford Female-fronted openers FRENZEE and The Belair Lip Bombs are a thoughtful balance to the masculinity marathon. Foo Fighters bear the weight of three hours – and 31 live-playing years – with power. Grohl is an impeccable frontman, who says f--- a lot, and motherf---er almost as much. His presence is amplified on towering screens, tracing neck muscles straining in each scream, chewing gum slipping between brilliantly bared teeth. Grohl swaggers with rockstar theatrics, flinging hair, chugging beer and breaking for wandering digressions that are charmingly, well, dad.

The production flashes with lightning-storm illumination and ever-changing video aesthetics: dreamy, distorted, scribble-scattered or bursting with colour. Even those at the back get one hell of a show. Classics deviate into fresh solos. The crowd collaborates, enunciating the anthemic Best of You and My Hero, stamping to the chugging riffs of Walk, carrying a constellation of phone lights in These Days. Foo Fighters has a muscular sound. Grohl can sustain screams but falters a little in quieter moments, straining for Under You, his melodies in This is a Call swallowed by guitar snarls and crashing drums. An exception is Aurora, played in honour of late drummer Taylor Hawkins, pensive sorrow-rock powered with gentle, earnest vocals. Ilan Rubin, Chris Shiflett and Pat Smear perform at Marvel Stadium on November 14, 2026. Richard Clifford Ilan Rubin is a captivating successor to Hawkins, from galloping beats and a mind-melting solo in No Son Of Mine to the hypnotic drive of Run. Drumroll attacks in Monkey Wrench are matched by frenzied cinematography, this possessed musical beast about to destroy himself. Grohl plays towards him, a mirroring of mop-haired, black-clad men. title: 'Reject any implications': Pat Cummins to remain Australia captain
text:
In brief Cricket Australia says it backs Pat Cummins as captain.

The organisation's board voted unanimously to keep him in the position.

Pat Cummins will remain Australia's Test captain despite controversy over his role in the sandpaper scandal.

Cummins' tenure as skipper had been questioned amid conflicting accounts of what he knew about Australia's ball tampering in the 2018 South African series.

Following a board meeting, Cricket Australia (CA) on Saturday confirmed Cummins would stay as captain for the three-Test series against New Zealand starting 9 December in Perth, issuing a statement rejecting any implication that his "integrity has been compromised".

"In the light of the ongoing speculation surrounding the Australian men's team tour of South Africa in 2018, the CA Board met to ensure measures are in place to protect the integrity of Australian cricket and the welfare of all concerned," CA wrote in a statement.

"As part of this meeting, the board resolved to express its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain given ongoing speculation about his position."

The statement revealed that CA chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg met with Cummins in Sydney on Friday.

That followed the announcement that players from the 2018 series would be invited to participate in an independent forum, that would allow them to give their accounts of the incident.

"We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa," Boon said.

"We have learned from that experience, and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised."

Cummins said he backed the forum and intended to participate.

"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there," the fast bowler said.

"All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations, but that is what's needed.

"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."

Cummins, who has held the captaincy since late November 2021, has steadfastly denied any knowledge of Australia's use of sandpaper on the ball in the 2018 series in South Africa.

His stance has been repudiated by Cameron Bancroft, Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers; all teammates of the paceman on the infamous tour eight years ago.

Cummins has described Khawaja's claims the entire touring party knew of scheming to tamper with the ball in South Africa as "nonsense" and has been backed Josh Hazlewood.

Hazelwood said he would have considered quitting if Cummins was made to stand down.

"I think I'd have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you'd have to think about it, yeah," Hazlewood told NewsCorp.

"It feels like it's been a bit of a pile on the last few days from different people. I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain.

"I think if we turned up for the first Test and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."

Meanwhile, Steve Smith will be back in the spotlight after being included in the NSW side for the final round of Sheffield Shield games before Australia name a squad for the New Zealand series.

The star batsman was stripped of the Test captaincy and received a 12-month ban from all international and Australian domestic cricket for his role in the cheating saga, but the 37-year-old has maintained his silence amid the fresh furore.

Smith hasn't played any cricket since suffering a neck injury in the second Test on last month's tour of South Africa, but was named in the Blues' squad for the SCG match against Queensland, starting Sunday.

He trained on Friday, but arrived through a back entrance and media were locked out of watching him bat in the nets.

Spinner Nathan Lyon, who was also part of the 2018 contingent was also included in the 12-man line-up, while other members of the national cohort Cummins, Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc were left out.

The Australian side will be named after the round of Shield games, with Western Australia also hosting Tasmania and South Australia at home to Victoria.

title: The traps, dodgy deals and scams to watch for this Black Friday and Cyber Monday
text:
In brief Many retailers have kicked off sales ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Consumer groups say it's important for shoppers to watch for a range of misleading sales tactics.

One of the biggest retail sales periods of the year is underway. But with it comes the risk of scams, misleading marketing and deals that aren't really deals.

The Australian consumer watchdog says it is monitoring websites, emails and social media for misleading sales advertising.

"Consumers continue to look for the best prices and may delay major purchases until Black Friday and Cyber Monday in anticipation of good value and legitimate discounts," Catriona Lowe, deputy chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), said earlier this month.

"Consumers should be able to trust that the advertised savings and discount prices are genuine, but we know some businesses use tactics to mislead consumers into thinking they are getting a bargain even when they are not."

Black Friday and Cyber Monday fall on 27 and 30 November this year, but many retailers have already kicked off their sales.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The ACCC said it is cracking down on misleading sales tactics, including "sitewide" discounts that exclude many products, limited-time offers that continue past their advertised end date, and false claims that stock is running low.

It is also scrutinising discounts advertised against prices that products were never — or have not recently been — sold at.

Here are some of the tactics bargain hunters should watch for.

Deadlines and timers

Setting deadlines is an "age-old trick" designed to rush shoppers into a purchase, according to financial comparison site Canstar.

During Black Friday and Cyber Monday, many sites use countdown timers showing how long shoppers have left to secure a deal.

Businesses are permitted to use these timers, but only if the deadline is genuine.

A number of major retailers were fined following the ACCC's sweep of last year's Black Friday sales advertising.

The ACCC alleged two of the businesses advertised that their sales would end at a certain time, but the discounts continued beyond that deadline.

One retailer offered an even bigger discount in a new sale after the earlier countdown ended, the watchdog said.

Scarcity warnings

Countdowns aren't the only way retailers create a sense of urgency.

Canstar also points to low-stock alerts such as "Hurry! Only two left in your size", virtual waiting rooms to access sales and messages suggesting multiple people are viewing an item.

These messages can make shoppers feel as though they need to act quickly or miss out.

Watch out for fine print

Stores will sometimes advertise deals of "up to 50 per cent off", but only discount a few items to that extent.

The detail clarifying that could be buried in a fine-print disclaimer.

The ACCC says retailers must ensure their sales and discount claims are clear and accurate, and that fine-print qualifications do not conflict with the overall message of the advertisement.

"Retailers should not be relying on fine print disclaimers or exclusions to qualify the headline message of a promotion," Lowe said.

Exaggerated savings

The watchdog will also be cracking down on ads that show misleading markdowns.

For example, if a retailer advertises that the price of a washing machine has been slashed from $500 down to $300, it suggests shoppers are saving $200.

But if the washing machine was recently priced at $400, the real saving compared with that price is only $100.

"Consumers are encouraged to focus on the end price of a product, not on promotional claims," the ACCC said.

"This includes checking for any exclusions or conditions, and comparing prices between retailers and over time where possible. They should carefully consider the advertised price and buy only if the price and time is right for them."

Scams

Buying and selling scams accounted for nearly 59 per cent of Scamwatch reports involving a financial loss in the first nine months of 2026.

These scams involve fraudsters posing as buyers or sellers to steal money, including through fake shopping websites and fraudulent profiles on legitimate platforms.

The government agency says scammers can look like businesses that you know and trust. Shoppers should be wary of social media stores selling products at very low prices, unfamiliar websites, and links received via email.

"Always check the web address, and if you don’t know the store, read reviews, or better yet, walk away," Canstar suggests.

title: Stocks tumble as AI bubble fears prompt market sell-off, with Anthropic shares falling
text:
In brief An AI bust in 2027 is a growing worry for investors.

AI firm Anthropic's share price has fallen after a bumper market debut.

Tech shares nosedived in the United States on Friday, local time, (Saturday AEDT) and dragged stocks into the red around the world, after AI firm Anthropic's bumper market debut failed to dispel growing worries about the sector's massive investments and sky-high valuations.

Anthropic shares briefly rocketed from an initial offering price of US $83 ($123) to over US $110 ($166) on Thursday despite a broader sell-off on Wall Street, but fell back sharply with the price plunging back below US $89 ($134) at the close on Friday.

"The performance of the shares over the coming days and weeks could provide one of the clearest tests yet of whether investors believe the enormous sums being poured into AI will ultimately generate attractive returns," Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said.

While Anthropic surged on its Nasdaq debut, the tech-dominated index struggled on Friday, closing down more than five per cent.

New York's broader S&P 500, which also trades the shares of the world's biggest tech companies, shed 3.7 per cent on Friday, extending a run of losses.

title: Trump's administration is sending mixed signals on chips, China and AI
text:
In brief The US is seeking to combat the spread of Chinese open-weight AI models and restrict access to high-end chips from US companies.

The Chinese embassy in Washington says China opposes politicising trade and tech issues, which will "serve no one's interests".

The United States approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced Nvidia and AMD chips to Chinese companies over six months, as the Trump administration reportedly considers requiring US firms to disclose their use of Chinese AI models.

The US House of Representatives' foreign affairs committee said on Friday that between December 2025 and May 2026, the US government approved 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD.

All four companies are on the Pentagon's list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies. The chips sold included Nvidia's H200 and AMD's equivalent MI325X chips.

Companies had sought permission to ship over 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the committee's documents showed. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of chips.

Former US president Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the chips over fears that they would supercharge China's military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Trump gave the green light in December for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to approved companies in China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.

The US commerce department said its approach to H200 licensing "is based on a rule published in the Federal Register in January 2026, which imposes significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial".

Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were "subject to strict conditions and limited volumes". The California-based company added that "despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China".

Meanwhile, AMD said it "complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations".

Earlier this week, the US said it would further restrict China's access to high-end chips from US companies, citing national security concerns and saying it would close "dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years".

The new rule restricts shipments of advanced chips to Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models.

The announcement came shortly after longtime Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company following reports he had an affair with a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that rents computing power at its data centres. The company has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of advanced AI chips to China.

US intelligence officials have alleged the woman was a Chinese spy, an accusation China has denied.

Before resigning as Nvidia CEO, Huang had lobbied the Trump administration to allow more of his company's chip sales to China, warning that the controls would otherwise boost the Chinese chip industry's competitiveness.

On Friday, California announced it was investigating whether Nvidia misled the public and investors about its chips ending up in China, despite federal export controls.

"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," US attorney-general Rob Bonta said in a statement.

'Name and shame' campaign

At the same time, the US is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, a bid to discourage reliance on the technology without imposing new restrictions that could anger industry or China, according to Reuters.

The US treasury department and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) have discussed the plan, which would apply to companies such as Airbnb.

The short-term rental platform uses Qwen, an AI model made by China's Alibaba, to power its AI customer service agent.

Under the plan, companies like Airbnb would be required to post that information on their websites.

It's unclear whether the idea is gaining traction within the administration or if it would be enshrined in a formal rulemaking process.

But its consideration underscores an emerging push by the US to combat the spread of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Open-weight models make their core components publicly available for anyone to download and adapt.

The proposal also shows officials are looking at ways to discourage use of Chinese AI through a "name and shame" campaign while sticking to a broader anti-regulation stance on AI.

Neither the White House, the US treasury department, nor Alibaba have commented on the proposal.

Airbnb said in a statement to Reuters that its AI activity "runs overwhelmingly on US-origin models" and the company uses "only a limited number of China-origin models, all of which are open-source and run only through approved US-based service providers, keeping data and operations separate and protected".

The Chinese embassy in Washington said China opposes politicising trade and tech issues, which will "only stifle global AI advances and serve no one's interests".

"We will resolutely safeguard Chinese businesses' lawful rights and interests," it said.

Chinese-made open-weight models are gaining ground with US companies because they are cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic.

But some within the US, including officials in Trump's administration, fear China is using such models — like Kimi, DeepSeek, or Qwen — to hook US companies into becoming dependent on Chinese AI.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said in July that the Trump administration could sanction Chinese AI companies if they were found to be guilty of intellectual property theft through distillation of US models.

Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using the output of larger ones to lower the cost of training a powerful new AI tool.

Bessent's remarks echoed comments in April by OTSP director Michael Kratsios, who accused China of stealing US artificial intelligence labs' intellectual property on an "industrial scale", spurring a push by the US state department to highlight such behaviour to foreign counterparts.

title: A decade on from Brexit, EU and UK relations reach a 'turning point'
text:
In brief The summit was part of efforts to forge a closer relationship, 10 years after the UK voted to leave the bloc.

Critics say Brexit has left the UK weaker and isolated.

The United Kingdom and the European Union have agreed to remove barriers to trade and expand travel opportunities for young people as they pledged to rebuild their strained ties with an "ambitious and dynamic" relationship.

But they left big decisions about softening or reversing Brexit for another day.

In a joint statement on Friday night AEDT after a summit in Brussels, the UK and EU confirmed agreements that will scrap border checks on plant and animal products, cut carbon taxes on some exports by linking their emissions trading schemes and let 100,000 young adults from each side live and work in the other's countries for up to three years.

Other areas remain a work in progress, with the two sides giving themselves six months to reach an agreement on the level of university fees for EU students in the UK and vice versa.

The summit was part of efforts to forge a closer relationship, a decade after the UK voted to leave the EU and six years after the divorce became final.

Supporters of Brexit argued that leaving the EU's vast free-trade area and web of rules would let the UK take back control of its borders, laws and economy, and strike new trade deals around the world.

Critics say Brexit has left the UK weaker and more isolated, and new deals with countries including Australia and Japan have not made up for the economic hit from erecting barriers between the UK and its closest and biggest economic partners.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the deal is "a turning point" in EU-UK relations, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it a "historic moment".

"This is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe," he said.

This was only the second EU-UK summit since the UK became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc. Months — likely years — of negotiations lie ahead on everything from electricity markets to manufacturing rules.

Burnham said the summit was a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.

He said the two sides are "rebuilding the bridges that were broken all of those years ago" and "building a much more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbors and our largest market".

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now 27-nation bloc.

READ MORE UK prime minister says Russia meddled in Brexit vote, pushes for EU return

But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of UK voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

"We remain open to have the closest possible relationship," European Council president António Costa said.

But he also recalled the obligations of EU membership, including single-market principles on the free movement of goods, services, people and capital.

Burnham says closer ties will ease the cost of living

Burnham pitched the package of agreements as a way of "cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people." He said the deals could bring in £17 billion ($33 billion) a year and add 0.5 per cent to the UK's economic output.

British retailers welcomed the deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products, which will make it cheaper and easier for UK businesses to export to Europe.

"Getting our spaghetti bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and even the Latin name of a cow," said Alex Freudmann, managing director of food at Marks and Spencer.

Freudmann said the announcement "is a major step forward".

But nothing in UK-EU relations is ever quick or simple. EU negotiators want European students to pay domestic fees if they study in the UK rather than the higher fees for foreign students, something the UK has resisted.

An EU official said negotiations had not been easy but they sensed good will to resolve the issue. The official was designated to brief reporters about the summit but only on condition that they not be named.

Talks are also continuing on the UK's desire to be included in the bloc’s "made in Europe" rules, which favor European manufacturers for public projects over rivals from China or elsewhere.

Critics say the deals are a betrayal of Brexit

To get the deals, the UK must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines the UK's independence.

Nigel Farage, leader of the euroskeptic, anti-immigration party Reform UK, told reporters in Brussels that Burnham had taken "the first step, incrementally, to take us back into membership of the European Union".

The war in Ukraine, and the UK's military strength, are drawing the two sides back together, and the summit produced pledges of stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the UK rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven UK prime ministers over the last decade and want clarity about the country’s intentions.

Von der Leyen said that a lot has changed in their relations since the Brexit vote, including the pandemic and Russia’s war on Ukraine. She said that the EU is "totally open to do the necessary brainstorming for the wider picture, the bigger picture" of what ties could look like in the future.

Burnham said he wanted the two sides to do that brainstorming before their next summit, probably a year from now.

For now, Burnham remains bound by the pledge made by Keir Starmer, his predecessor as Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or friction-less single market, or to restore free movement for EU nationals to the UK

He acknowledged the agreements are "the limit of what we can achieve" before a national election.

title: The controversial export title Australia is on track to earn
text:
In Brief A new report from the International Energy Agency shows Australia set to become the world's biggest coal exporter.

The organisation said uptake in renewables will continue to grow in coming decades.

Australia could become the world's largest exporter of coal within the next decade, according to analysis from an international energy body.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has published its annual World Energy Outlook since 1999, offering multiple views of potential energy futures based on that year's developments.

In this year's report, the agency provided a cautious view based on current policies, another based on policies announced but not yet enacted and a third more ambitious view seeking to reduce emissions alongside alternatives for potential impacts of the conflict in the Middle East.

Since the organisation was established in 1974, energy demand has nearly tripled worldwide. Coal has been the fastest-growing fossil fuel since 2020, with Indonesia and Australia among the top exporters.

By 2035, this would make Australia the largest supplier of coal, with the margin growing further by 2050.

Alongside the growth in renewable energy production, the oil and gas supply shock has accelerated solar, battery and electric vehicle adoption in several countries.

title: Why our World War Two-era recession formula 'doesn't speak to reality'
text:
In brief The federal government and Reserve Bank have denied Australia will enter a recession, despite economic pressures.

Some economists endorse unemployment as the best indicator of a recession, with one saying GDP is an outdated measure.

Australian households are facing increasing financial pressure, with interest rates, inflation and unemployment on the rise. Despite the squeeze, Australia isn't expected to enter a recession.

The federal government has denied Australia is heading towards recession, with Treasurer Jim Chalmers naming rising interest rates and the war in Iran as major contributors to mounting economic pressure.

Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler told Sunrise recent figures "show the pressure the economy is under".

"We're not predicting a recession. The Reserve Bank's not predicting a recession either," he said.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) describes a recession as a sustained period of weak or negative growth in gross domestic product (GDP) accompanied by a significant rise in unemployment.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Currently, Australia's GDP is rising, but employment is falling.

Australia's GDP grew to 0.4 per cent in the June 2026 quarter, up from 0.3 per cent in the March quarter — and the national GDP slowed from 2.5 per cent in March to 2.1 per cent in June.

Unemployment hit its highest rate in five years in October, rising to 4.9 per cent – up from 4.1 per cent in January.

There remains no formal economic definition of recession. The RBA refers to a 'technical recession' defined by "two consecutive quarters of negative growth in real GDP".

"Whenever you put technical in front of something, it does kind of give away the fact it's an arbitrary measure that doesn't speak to the reality of what might be going on," Greg Jericho, chief economist at left-wing thinktank The Australia Institute, told SBS News.

However, Jericho warns that Australia's method for defining a recession may be outdated — and thus unable to properly determine one.

Is GDP an appropriate indicator for modern economies?

Jericho said the measure of "two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth" worked well post-World War Two, when there were "manufacturing economies".

He says Australia is now a "service economy" which relies heavily on mining and mining exports.

If an international company exports mined resources from Australia, those exports count towards the nation's GDP figures, Jericho said.

However, the industry doesn't have a high employment rate.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics' Labour Force Survey from February 2026, 314,500 Australians work directly in the mining industry — 2.1 per cent of the national workforce.

"So, Australia may have exported a lot of iron ore in one quarter, which helped us stay out of recession, but you or I don't necessarily get any money from iron ore," he said.

The artificial intelligence industry is similar.

"The GDP might be fine because we have the AI investment boom, but it's not providing many jobs, no more income, and it's certainly not driving wage growth," Jericho said.

"It might take us out of that technical recession — but who cares?"

Another issue with a GDP-based assessment of recession is that it's "woefully slow" and GDP figures are often revised, Jericho said.

He said data from two quarters isn't confirmed until "six months after the fact".

Jericho said the GDP is "quite divorced from what people are feeling".

"During the global financial crisis, we didn't have two quarters of consecutive GDP growth, but the unemployment rate rose very quickly — over a percentage point in a year," he said.

"People would have felt very much like it was a recession."

He said Australia's Reserve Bank has "consistently" misread the economy this year.

"They were expecting unemployment to hit 4.9 per cent in December next year ... Three months ago, they thought unemployment by now would be just 4.5 per cent," he said.

"It really highlights that their belief that the economy needs to be slowed by more rate rises was completely wrong."

An employment-based definition?

Former US Federal Reserve economist Claudia Sahm coined the Sahm rule, which says a recession starts when the three-month moving average of the national unemployment rate rises by 0.5 percentage points or more above its lowest level over the prior 12 months.

"By her measure, Australia is pretty much right there," Jericho said.

He said that using Sahm's rule is a proactive option.

Jericho said if unemployment is rising by more than half a per cent in a year, it "keeps going up pretty fast and later lines up with GDP going backwards".

He said acting quickly to address unemployment is crucial to reversing recession.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said the October labour force data would be the start of an upward trend in unemployment.

"It's probably a sign of things to come," he told Australian Associated Press.

"The number of job losses reported ... reflect the slowdown in the economy on the back of rate hikes, cost-of-living pressures, poor confidence and so on."

Oliver said the rise was a sign the Reserve Bank's five interest rate hikes in 2026 had worked their way through the economy.

But the moves to slow inflation had led to higher unemployment, which in turn boosted the chances of a recession.

"I'd say the risk is high. It's around 40 per cent," he said.

Jericho maintains that Australia hasn't entered a recession yet. But if unemployment reaches 5 per cent, it would be "really hard to argue that we're not".

The Reserve Bank earlier in November revised its unemployment forecast for the jobless rate to reach five per cent by 2028.

Independent economist Saul Eslake said that figure was more likely to be reached early in 2027.

"These numbers, for the time being at least, further downplay the likelihood of another increase in interest rates in December, and arguably also reduce the probability of another rate hike in February," he said.

October inflation data, due to be released on Wednesday, is likely to confirm the next move by the Reserve Bank's board.

Eslake said future unemployment numbers could be a harbinger of a recession.

— With reporting by the Australian Associated Press

The property was one of 984 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 47 per cent from 560 reported results throughout the week, while 225 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The result is a modest increase on last week’s early read of 45 per cent, the equal lowest preliminary result this year, but remains well below the threshold of 60 per cent that indicates a market balanced between buyers and sellers.

Advertisement

The Kirribilli home, known in the area as “the blue house”, had a price guide of $8.5 million and attracted two bidders at auction. Related Article Auctions ‘Quality home’: Paddington terrace sells for $310,000 above reserve Bidding began at $8.35 million and rose fast at first. Proceedings slowed once the price reached $8.5 million, which was also the reserve price, and from there the parties traded $10,000 bids, The Agency selling agent Sandro Petrini said. The winners are a local owner-occupier couple who used to live nearby and missed living there, he said. “It is one of those unique houses, everyone calls it ‘the blue house’, everyone loves it that lives there locally.”

Advertisement

He said the winning bidders were in Madrid, where it was the middle of the night, and bidding by phone. The underbidders were from the lower north shore. He thought if the market was stronger there might have been another two, three or four bidders for the home. “It is just a unique home,” Petrini said. “It is private because it is a diamond-shaped block.” He said the home was in great condition, noting the cornices, ceilings and three-car garage. “The formal part of it is sensational and then you have got the more modern part as well.”

Advertisement

Asked about the market in general, he described conditions as “terrible”, then reflected. “It is not terrible, it is just, the buyers are very nervous, that is all,” he said. “This is the best time to be buying.” In Strathfield, a contemporary architect-designed home sold for $9.6 million after four parties registered and all four of them bid. The five-bedroom home at 61 Cotswold Road featured natural stone, a butler’s pantry, a swimming pool and outdoor dining area. The first bid was $8.7 million and the price rose in increments of $100,000 to start, then $50,000.

Advertisement

The home sold under the hammer for its reserve price of $9.6 million, which was also the price guide, to a local family who are upsizing. The vendors are also upsizing to a bigger block in the same suburb. Related Article Title Deeds Rock star sells Point Piper apartment after years-long campaign McGrath Strathfield selling agent Tarun Sethi thought the home stood out for its construction quality and its location in the “Golden Mile” of Strathfield. He thought the market broadly was performing well, noting his team has sold $41 million of Strathfield real estate in the last four days. “The market seems to be fairly strong in Strathfield still, despite a lot of the noise,” he said.

Advertisement

“Around the market, people are realising that if they don’t buy now, they might catch themselves buying in the upswing in the next year.” He noted the rise in unemployment in the latest jobs data, which he thought made it unlikely there would be further interest rate hikes. In Concord, a man paid $1.68 million for a fixer-upper that also had the potential to become a site for a new dream home. The three-bedroom house at 4 Spring Street had a price guide of $1.7 million and attracted five registered bidders, of whom four were active.

Advertisement

Bidding opened at $1.5 million and rose at first in $50,000 bids, followed by $25,000 and eventually increments of $5000. The reserve price was $1.65 million. Related Article Sydney house prices ‘The downturn’s broadened’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.66m Dib Chidiac of DibChidiac&Co handled the sale and said the buyers were young locals who will build a family home. The property was a deceased estate being sold by the executors. Auctioneer Clarence White of Menck White Auctioneers thought the owner was well aligned to market conditions. “We sold below the guide. Some owners are, at the moment,” he said. “It was not unexpected. It would have been nice to get a little bit more.”

Advertisement

He thought the location was a good spot to do a building project as it is close to shops and amenities. He described the market as challenging, with the odd standout auction. “Buyers are super price cautious, they are super price sensitive, they don’t want to pay one dollar more than they have to,” he said. BusinessConsumer affairsBlack Friday Fake websites, GTA 6 scams: What you shouldn’t click on this Black Friday Jessica Yun November 22, 2026 — 3:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Black Friday bargain hunters have been urged to stay alert for counterfeit shopfronts and AI-generated content as the national scams agency observes a global rise in deepfake content. Cybersecurity experts and consumer protection agencies have warned against lookalike websites masquerading as legitimate brands spruiking too-good-to-be-true deals, as the nation is forecast to spend a record $7.2 billion in the four days between Black Friday on November 27 and Cyber Monday on the 30th. Black Friday is one of the biggest shopping events of the year. AP The National Anti-Scam Centre (NASC), a consumer protection body that sits within the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, said law enforcement partners, regulators and global counterparts had all observed a global rise in artificial intelligence tools being exploited to create highly realistic, personalised websites, particularly in online shopping and investment. “The National Anti-Scam Centre has observed more concerns and reports this year about AI-cloned storefronts, deepfake brand or celebrity ads, and ‘news’ items,” a spokesperson said in a statement to this masthead.

Advertisement

More than one in two (58.7 per cent) of all Scamwatch reports in the first nine months of this year were buying and selling scams. More than 11,500 victims lost $17.2 million during this period, according to NASC figures. Related Article Black Friday 16 of the best Christmas gifts to shop on Amazon during the Black Friday sales Common scams can include shops claiming to go out of business and giving away items free of charge, or websites that have poorer-quality images or incomplete information. Shoppers should be wary of websites that appear to have AI-generated images or video or missing basic business or contact information. Check the retailer’s official website instead of responding to unsolicited messages or links in texts or emails. “Fake shops and fake sales are among the biggest issues, and they invariably increase just before major holidays,” said Bitdefender cybersecurity specialist Silviu Stahie. “A fairly typical example in Australia is ads for shops that are going out of business and clearing their stock, with items given away free of charge.” Scammers will be attempting to capitalise on a false sense of urgency and FOMO (fear of missing out), which are already heightened in a sales environment.

Advertisement

“Black Friday is particularly ripe for this because shoppers are expecting to be bombarded with ads, flash deals and messages telling them to act quickly,” said ING head of consumer insights Matt Bowen. Popular games with a global cult following like Grand Theft Auto VI can make victims of those who fall for offers that look convincing. Malicious actors have been caught selling PC versions of the game, which doesn’t exist. “Scammers are very good at following the hype,” added Bowen. “If you suddenly see offers for exclusive access, heavily discounted copies, downloads or giveaways, particularly through an unexpected ad or link, it’s worth taking a moment to check that it’s legitimate and going directly to the official retailer.” Well-known retailers offering deep discounts of 50 to 90 per cent off should be viewed with some wariness, as should congratulatory messages claiming the consumer has won a reward or prize. “If something seems too good to be true, it probably is,” said digital safety software platform TrendLife head of consumer education Lynette Owens. “And if an offer is too tempting to turn down, always check the brand’s official pages and channels to confirm if the deal is real.”

Advertisement

Courier and postal service scams are always rife at this time of year, with Australia Post, FedEx and DHL frequently impersonated from Black Friday throughout the holiday season, she warned. “It’s the busiest time of the year for deliveries, and cyber criminals are watching for any chance to exploit your eagerness to receive your parcels.” Related Article Black Friday Watchdog warns retailers over fake Black Friday deals and false urgency The ACCC is watching Shoppers have learned to expect deals and markdowns well before Black Friday, which typically falls on the last Friday of November. On average, Australian retailers are kicking off Black Friday sales about two weeks earlier, with delivery platform Shippit seeing 10 per cent more online orders than the same period last year. The consumer watchdog has warned retailers against misleading practices, including “sitewide” or “storewide” claims that actually exclude several products, time-limited offers, false claims about remaining stock that pressure shoppers into purchasing, and was/now prices in which those items were never or not recently sold at those prices.

Advertisement

The ACCC’s 2025 Black Friday sweep of 50 retailers saw James Lane and Vuly penalised nearly $60,000 for creating a false sense of urgency, while Booktopia owner digiDirect paid $99,000 for misleading was/now claims. This year, the maximum corporate penalty for retailers falling foul of Australian consumer law has doubled from $50 million to $100 million per contravention. “Retailers need to be careful about creating a false sense of urgency with claims such as ‘ends today’, ‘last chance’ or countdown timers, particularly if the same discounts continue or the sale is extended,” said law firm Holding Redlich special counsel Emily Booth. “There is also a risk that a ‘sale’ price effectively becomes the standard price.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
