title: This is a tale that many may not know well, but its consequences are still felt today
text:
Advertisement

Key points OPERA: Opera Australia bring Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan to Melbourne

JAZZ: The Vampires perform at Bennetts Lane Jazz Club

MUSIC: ACO finishes the season on a high note with Beethoven’s Pastoral

THEATRE: Novel, movie and now a play: A Room With A View comes to MTC

MUSIC: Aldous Harding performs to a sold out crowd at Forum Melbourne

OPERA

Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan ★★★

Playhouse, Arts Centre Melbourne, until November 28 A man is suspended in mid-air above a body of water that stretches across the stage. He descends, drowning as he falls. It’s a visceral opening, the ensuing tale one that Australians may not know well, but the consequences of which are still felt today. Sebastian Geilings is gut-wrenchingly stunning in Opera Australia’s Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan. Ben Fon Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan first premiered at the Adelaide Festival in 2022. It is a work by Brisbane composer Joseph Twist and librettists Alana Valentine and Christos Tsiolkas, the production devised by Neil Armfield. Opera Australia now brings Watershed to the Arts Centre. We begin with the 1972 death of Dr George Duncan, who drowned in Adelaide’s River Torrens. Herein lies the “watershed”. It’s this tragic event that leads to the decriminalisation of homosexual acts in South Australia. We agonisingly watch as three police officers are tried and acquitted in relation to Dr Duncan’s death.

Advertisement

The crime remains unsolved. The subject matter is deeply serious and is intended to be confronting. Anyone familiar with Tsiolkas – known for his colloquialisms and liberal use of profanity – might have known what was coming. Watershed: The Death of Dr Duncan Ben Fon Coupled with the experience of Valentine, a doyenne of verbatim theatre (where transcripts of real people are taken and morphed into, usually, a play), the libretto is plainly, astonishingly blue. Which is certainly what 1970s Adelaideans would have sounded like, but when language is so naturalistic yet sung operatically (the most unnaturalistic), an unintended side effect that can sneak in is caricature. At times, this plot, involving a real person’s life lost in devastating circumstances, felt trivialised.

Advertisement

Joseph Twist is known to those of us with young children as a composer on Bluey, but his music crosses all boundaries. With influences of Bach, Sondheim, Pink Floyd and others, this score feels closer to musical theatre than oratorio, as it is referred to in the program. What it isn’t, is opera. Whether anyone cares about that is in the eye of the beholder. Musical theatre tenor Blake Appelqvist takes on the main role of the Lost Boy, and does so with deft sweetness, though their voice lacks resonance. Geilings with Blake Appelqvist as Lost Boy. Ben Fon The chorus are the real stars; Twist gives them layers upon layers of harmonies, with various moments for individual choristers to shine. Sebastian Geilings, the aforementioned dangling dancer, is gut-wrenchingly stunning. Though the period-ambiguous costumes did not aid the storytelling, Armfield’s direction is clever and undoubtedly powerful. After more than 50 years, this story deserves the spotlight, and many will be moved by it, no matter the manner in which it is told.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

JAZZ

The Vampires ★★★★

Bennetts Lane Jazz Club, November 21 At a time when the Australian music industry is facing multiple challenges – rising costs, insecure conditions and the existential threat of AI – it’s heartening to see a queue snaking down the street outside a local jazz club. The Vampires are a band whose warmth is key to their sonic signature. It’s even more heartening to see a new venue open when so many are closing, and to see it filled to the rafters for a concert by a long-running Australian jazz quartet. Sydney band The Vampires tour here regularly, but this was their first show in The JazzLab’s newly unveiled second room (named Bennetts Lane after owner Michael Tortoni’s previous club in the CBD), with excellent acoustics and twice the capacity of JazzLab.

Advertisement

Those acoustics served the band well on Saturday night at the Melbourne launch of their latest album, Skydancer. On the recording, all four players added extra layers and electronic effects in post-production. On stage, they layered and processed the sound in real time, enhancing the music’s textural depth without ever smothering its warmth. Related Article Melbourne live reviews My Fair Lady has arrived, and it’s an abso-bloomin’-lutely loverly treat That’s crucial for a band whose warmth is key to its sonic signature, along with memorable twin-horn themes and loping, dub-inflected grooves. Saxophonist Jeremy Rose and trumpeter Nick Garbett both used pedals to add reverb and delay to their instruments, but it was the creativity of their interactions – dancing in relaxed unison or taut harmonic lines, and engaging in energetic, improvised conversations – that made the music feel alive. Noel Mason could alter the tone of his electric bass at will (fat and insistent, or light and guitaristic), but could also switch to acoustic bass for a brighter, breezier sound. And while drummer Alex Masso added an occasional touch of reverb to his snare, it was the invention of his touch that provided the music’s rhythmic vitality, via languid backbeats, polyrhythmic shuffles or a swift, heady propulsion. Now in their 21st year, The Vampires are still finding new ways to expand their creative vision, without losing sight of the approachability – and humanity – that makes their music so appealing.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas

Advertisement

MUSIC

Beethoven’s Pastoral ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, November 21 It was a triple treat in more ways than one. For its final national tour of the year, the Australian Chamber Orchestra served up a winning trifecta of contrasting Beethoven works: the Coriolan Overture, the “Triple Concerto” and the “Pastoral” Symphony. Beethoven’s Pastoral was an uplifting end to another fruitful ACO season. Nic Walker Another treat was hearing the trio of lead violinist Richard Tognetti, principal cellist Timo-Veikko Valve and pianist Konstantin Shamray perform together as soloists in the unjustly neglected concerto. Forming a seamless prelude to the concerto’s quiet opening was the high drama of the Coriolan Overture. Thrumming with energy, the music was initially discharged in high-voltage chords before Tognetti ensured ongoing phrasing was flexible and well shaped.

Advertisement

There could have been no better way to celebrate Valve’s 20 years with the ACO than to collaborate with his friends in Beethoven’s charming amalgam of chamber and concerto styles. In all three movements, the cello has a starring role introducing the solo material and the golden, honeyed tone Valve’s Amati instrument made for unalloyed listening pleasure. Shamray’s use of a modern concert grand made perfect sense against an augmented ACO. Joined with Tognetti’s brighter-toned Guarneri del Gesù and period wind and brass, the entire ensemble filled Elisabeth Murdoch Hall with an impressive heft, warmth and clarity that could only be totally appreciated in person. Full of inventive detours, the concerto’s concluding Rondo alla Polacca made for an ebullient finale. Tognetti and his players gave a distinctly evocative account of Beethoven’s idyllic symphony; the period wind and brass giving the familiar music added piquancy. Ernst Schlader’s clarinet was a constant joy while the valveless horns were almost always stirring. Beethoven’s many contrasts were well pointed, not least the transition from the rustic country dancing into the ensuing thunderstorm and the eventual thanksgiving of the shepherds. What an uplifting end to another fruitful ACO season.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

THEATRE

A Room with a View ★★★

Melbourne Theatre Company, Southbank Theatre, until December 19 The first question the trepidatious theatregoer who has read E.M. Forster’s 1908 novel and seen the 1985 Merchant Ivory movie adaptation will ask is: do we even need a stage version? Nathalie Morris and Luke Wiltshire in A Room with a View. Brett Boardman It’s certainly treacherous territory to approach a much-loved classic with the aim of revitalising it for a new audience, and this iteration is an uneven one – not quite a tribute to the original text nor a wholesale modernisation. Adapted by Grace Chapple and directed by Hannah Goodwin, A Room with a View follows the convoluted getting-of-wisdom path of Lucy Honeychurch (Nathalie Morris) as she travels from England to Italy with her companion-chaperone cousin Charlotte (Hayley McElhinney).

Advertisement

Charlotte’s minder role seems to be a proprietary and protective one: to be in charge of Lucy’s moral education. After all, the Edwardian era dictates that a young, wealthy, unmarried woman of a certain class must conduct herself with decorum – which certainly does not extend to fraternising with men of questionable, socialist backgrounds. When Lucy meets and finds herself attracted to George Emerson (Luke Wiltshire) in Florence, she slowly begins to unbutton herself to possibilities beyond those predetermined for her. In terms of social standing, and despite his pomposity, Cecil Vyse (Charles Wu), a family friend, is a far more appropriate partner, but George offers a sense of the unknown, of freedom. Luke Wiltshire as George Emerson. Brett Boardman Wu brings an energy to him that’s not present in Wiltshire until the later scenes; so too does Tomáš Kantor, who doubles as Lucy’s exuberant brother Freddy and as an Italian driver. The rest of the cast acquit themselves well, including McElhinney’s turn as the shrewish, gossipy Charlotte and Tom Conroy as the vicar with secrets of his own. Chapple’s script moves from first-person dialogue to third-person narration, giving us both the individual and the omniscient perspective. Lucy’s sexual awakening is gradual and mired in confusion and self-deception.

Advertisement

Morris offers a spirited, open-eyed performance as she experiences the frisson of the new. But Wiltshire’s performance feels lacklustre next to her. Their budding relationship never feels genuinely lit up, and part of the problem lies with the disappointing, sparse set, which is primarily made up of a series of window frames upon which various scenes are projected – none memorable. The novel and the film both credit the glamour and radiance of Italy as pivotal to Lucy’s ripening – her falling into the throes of romance, but here such golden-lit vistas are missing. The set of A Room with a View is sparse. Brett Boardman There are no costuming updates; the production sticks to Edwardian period-appropriate clothing. However, there are some innovations to this adaptation that playfully lend themselves to theatricality, with various set pieces (a tennis match and the infamous lakeside skinny-dipping) that are wordless but dynamic and fun. While there are times when the momentum flags and it feels like there’s too much unnecessary exposition on the choices laid out for Lucy, one of the most poignant scenes is right towards the end, when McElhinney has her back to the audience and is looking out a window, her arms raised, leading us to wonder: will Charlotte ever have a possibility of choice like Lucy, a view of her choosing?

Reviewed by Thuy On

Advertisement

MUSIC

Aldous Harding ★★★★

Forum Melbourne, November 18 Tonight, New Zealand-born folk-pop songwriter Aldous Harding and her band spend most of the show sitting, meaning a lot of my view is the backs of people’s heads. If I angle it right, and the ocean of people sways in the right direction, I can see her, acoustic guitar in hand. But now what? Aldous Harding performs at the Forum. Richard Clifford Seeing her isn’t important tonight, and neither is small talk. Harding is no showboat. Between songs, she and the band mill silently, changing instruments, tuning. The audience wait patiently. The music converges somewhere over our heads. There’s plenty to fill the void left in place of sight lines and audience chatter. Harding’s songs are oblique. Much of tonight’s set is from her new album, Train on the Island.

Advertisement

Its songs are strange little machines, full of memorable images and unpredictable structures. She offers them with no context. “Mummy said my inception was like eating a pearl,” she sings on title track Train on the Island, over piano like knots in silk. Several tracks spin off into tangential outros, like on tonight’s highlight, If Lady Does It. The lyrics might be very personal, but she keeps herself at a tantalising distance. “This one’s about me,” she says in the introduction to Coats, but the chorus goes “Big thick coats on the dogs of people just trying to help.” Happily, we learn nothing tangible. Aldous Harding’s lyrics might be very personal, but she keeps herself at a tantalising distance. Richard Clifford “What is that accent?” my friend says during Leathery Whip. It’s no accent. It coils around Kiwi, American and something Germanic. These songs are from her subconscious, and she speaks her own language there. The sold-out crowd is mostly reverent, but silence invites people to fill it. A man yelps something incomprehensible. “So funny,” Harding almost whispers, dismissively. One fan yells out a too-complicated, impassioned plea that the lighting balance is wrong. “I can’t hear you, mate,” says Harding, and launches into Worms (“I flew down to the brewery / All wool dead on my waist”).

Advertisement

“You’ll be all right,” she says later. “I know the quiet is hard.” Related Article Visual art This artist wants you to leave her exhibition feeling odd – and ‘squished’ Harding closes her set with an encore of some older songs, Imagining My Man, with its twee little “Hey!” yelp, and the uncharacteristically sunny Designer (“Do not lose your young eyes / Laughing at good work with your ugly son”). As we leave, I hear a few people saying it would have been a perfect show if she played The Barrel, and if they could have seen her. I say embrace the obscured vision. There’s irreplicable joy in standing in silence with this many people, trying to get a glimpse at something you’ll never quite see and never quite understand.

Reviewed by Will Cox

Advertisement

MUSIC

Anne Sofie von Otter and Kristian Bezuidenhout ★★★★

Classical Music Australia, Melbourne Recital Centre, November 18 Swedish mezzo-soprano Anne Sofie von Otter has returned to Melbourne with the world-class stagecraft that has characterised her stellar career. Swedish mezzo-soprano Anne Sofie von Otter Presenting 16 Schubert songs with pianist Kristian Bezuidenhout, von Otter impressed an appreciative audience by bringing her compelling storytelling skills to the composer’s unique world where happiness and sadness, hope and disappointment are codependent. Schubert’s famous trout featured early on, along with revelling impish spirits in The Ghost Dance.

Advertisement

Further evidence of von Otter’s chameleonic versatility came with a gentle Lullaby, D. 867, the lyrical solemnity of Mignon’s Let Me Appear So, D. 877 and the effective use of her rich lower register in the nocturnal rustlings of In the Forest, D. 708. Related Article Melbourne live reviews Jason Donovan makes Ken Kesey’s iconic ‘bull goose loony’ his own Bezuidenhout’s solo interludes included an engrossing account of Mozart’s bittersweet Rondo in A minor, K. 511, very aligned with the Schubertian mood, while later came a spiky reading of Schubert’s Hungarian Melody in B minor, D. 817 and the long melodic arcs of the second-movement allegretto from the Piano Sonata in A minor, D. 537. In a lighter vein, four varied songs by von Otter’s 19th-century compatriot Adolf Lindblad proved a good foil for the final bracket of seven songs from Schwanengesang, D. 957, in which von Otter laid bare the stark anguish of unrequited love. Among Schubert’s last utterances, these songs include the popular Ständchen and Abschied, in which von Otter put on the lover’s brave face, while with Die Stadt and Der Doppelgänger came a confronting rawness.

Advertisement

Supported by Bezuidenhout’s empathy and dexterity, von Otter’s highly developed musicianship kept the focus on musical communication rather than on any understandable mellowing of her famously lustrous instrument. Two poignant encores, Schubert’s Lachen und Weinen and the ’60s hit Try to Remember, summed up the mood created by a memorable encounter with a great singer.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

title: Las Vegas F1 GP LIVE: Piastri’s masterful drive from 17th to the podium as Verstappen shines in Vegas
text:
In the middle of the nail-biting Las Vegas Grand Prix, Oscar Piastri’s race was looking entirely mediocre, and borderline bleak.

The Australian driver had started in 17th place (after a grid penalty during qualifying) and had fought his way up the grid.

But multiple crashes and yellow flags bunched the drivers from nose-to-tail on track, leaving Piastri marooned in 11th.

The design and nature of the Las Vegas circuit led to some of the closest, nail-biting racing of 2026. Getty Images

He and Lando Norris were, as McLaren CEO Zak Brown plainly put it, “sitting ducks”.

Then everything changed.

After the restart Piastri executed sensational moves on Pierre Gasly and both Ferraris, storming away to fifth place. Next, he overtook Kimi Antonelli, but couldn’t match the Mercedes pace and dropped back.

McLaren issued Piastri a warning, reminding him that although he was doing a “great job” he needed to be “careful around his teammate”, Lando Norris, who was ahead of him.

Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris John Locher/Pool AP via AP

“Stop f-—ing telling me to be careful,” he said over the radio.

Undeterred, Piastri stayed close to the pack, waiting for the right moment.

Then it arrived.

With four laps to go, Piastri pounced on his teammate near Turn 5 snatching fourth place.

Then after fighting Max Verstappen and teammate Kimi Antonelli for the lead for nearly 47 laps, Russell locked up and went into the barriers.

Piastri found himself in third, but quickly lost his podium position to Norris who pounced.

But then Antonelli – who claimed the championship – faltered, and Piastri and Norris both swooped, claiming third and second respectively.

Nearly six and a half months since he last podium in Miami, Oscar Piastri’s drought was over.

As fireworks exploded over Sin City, Piastri beamed and looked lost for words.

“They say Las Vegas is the entertainment capital of the world, and I think that was pretty entertaining,” he said.

“Obviously starting from the back, I didn’t know how it was going to go… I could kind of work out pretty early on that it was just staying as one massive pack.”

The Las Vegas Grand Prix had 35 lead changes across 50 laps. It was as Lando Norris aptly put, “the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1”.

It’s a spectacular achievement for Piastri who has struggled with poor luck, performance and pace in 2026, crashing out of his home grand prix in Melbourne and suffering several DNF’s.

A podium is preciously what the Australian needed heading into the off-season.

It was carnage and devastation for George Russell who battled for the race win all day, only to come up short with two laps to go.

“This sort of race it was high-risk and high reward.… the lock-up, it was unavoidable, obviously disappointing, but I don’t regret it,” Russell said in a post-race interview.

The only drivers having a worse day were Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

The duo have bristled over the last few months, with Ferrari failing to implement strict rules on inter-team racing.

Tensions boiled over during the Las Vegas Grand Prix with Hamilton fumed over the radio, saying “Charles is just… Can you tell him to back the f--- off,”

Later in the race, the duo collided, with Hamilton spinning off track.l Leclerc later received a 10 second-time penalty for causing the collision.

The 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix will probably go down in history as the race that had it all; teammate skirmishes, crashes, and miraculous podium positions.

title: My Fair Lady has arrived, and it’s an abso-bloomin’-lutely loverly treat
text:
Advertisement

Key points MUSICAL THEATRE: My Fair Lady arrives at Arts Centre Melbourne

DANCE: [gameboy] at Dancehouse is a delightfully twisted dance satire

MUSIC: Opera Australia brings The Trumpet of the Swan to Regent Theatre

MUSIC: Foo Fighters put on three hours of rock’n’roll at Marvel Stadium

MUSICAL THEATRE

My Fair Lady ★★★★

Ian Potter State Theatre, until January 17 It’s been 70 years since My Fair Lady made its Broadway debut, and now it’s also opening in the brand-new, refurbished Ian Potter State Theatre. There’s a nice poetic twist to this production, as it’s based on the 2016 version, where Julie Andrews was at the directorial helm. Reg Livermore (centre) and the cast of My Fair Lady. Joe Armao Andrews was the original Eliza Doolittle, the impoverished Cockney flower girl who, with linguistic training, a new wardrobe and some etiquette lessons, was transformed into an aristocrat, fashionably fit to be presented to society. It’s a musical about the shape-changing potential of language, class and deportment in terms of social climbing – but most importantly, of realising your own self-worth. In this revival, director Karen Johnson Mortimer works with Andrews’ original staging. Based on George Bernard Shaw’s 1912 play, Pygmalion, the story has always been misogynistic and offensive when you strip it down to its bones: a young woman becomes a pawn, a game between two men who argue about whether she could be elevated by manipulating her speech and elocution and then presenting her for public approval as though she were a project they were tinkering with simply to amuse themselves.

Advertisement

The gender politics may be dated, but there’s no argument against the entertainment factor of gutter-to-ball transformation, nor the enduring quality of some of the songs in My Fair Lady. Judging by the reception on opening night, most of the audience knew all the lyrics to I Could Have Danced All Night, The Rain in Spain, On the Street Where You Live and Get Me to the Church on Time. Visually, it’s an abso-bloomin’-lutely loverly treat. This is a big, non-stinting, lavish production with live orchestra accompaniment; the costume design (particularly in the black-and-white Ascot event) is as gorgeous as you’d expect, and the sets, with their painted backdrops and architectural rendering, are detailed and sumptuous, from the bustling street scenes of Covent Garden to the chandeliered Embassy ballroom. Claire Lyon makes a feisty Eliza Doolittle. Joe Armao Claire Lyon makes a feisty Eliza; her metamorphosis from scrappy ingenue to someone wiser and jaded is seeded in emotional growth. Beneath the winsome charm, there’s a steeliness to her that Lyon manages to coax out. She realises that societal acceptance and social mobility are more complicated than just the ability to round your vowels and wear a fabulous frock. Colonel Pickering (Tony Llewellyn-Jones) and Henry Higgins, Professor of Phonetics (Nathaniel Parker), are both suitably pompous and avuncular; the bantering between them is easy and affectionate.

Advertisement

Parker has the difficult role of playing a charismatic bully but manages to negotiate the balance. Eliza’s father, Alfred (Reg Livermore), is an energetic livewire whose physicality belies his age, and Freddy Hellier as Eliza’s suitor is peppy and sweet. As Mrs Higgins, Robyn Nevin’s performance imperiously and wittily counterbalances the behaviour of her abrasive son, and Anne Wood as the housekeeper, imbues a commanding presence. The Ascot scene in particular is a visual highlight. Joe Armao Though this production is a homage to the original, the ending may be problematic for a modern audience hoping for a feminist reworking, as it leans toward the familiar tropes of reconciliation, romance and capitulation, rather than self-possession and emancipation – as conceived by Shaw who fought against a happy-ending pairing between the professor and his student. But regardless of its sexist undertones, My Fair Lady is musical theatre gold, and decades later, its lustre still shines brightly. Eliza’s real education is not on learning how to speak, but how to be heard.

Reviewed by Thuy On

Advertisement

DANCE

[gameboy] ★★★★

Dancehouse, until November 21 With its ritual humiliations and painful stunts, this delightfully twisted dance satire by choreographer Amy Zhang revels in the pointless masochism of so many viral internet videos. Funny but disturbing, it’s a work possessed by thoroughly unwholesome desires and impulses. [gameboy] by Amy Zhang Daniel Boud The show opens with a quote from American singer-songwriter Raveena: “The internet is like eating plastic.” It’s a complaint that could be read as a gloss for the whole performance. Online obsessions can fill up a life while offering little nourishment to the spirit. Zhang gives that appetite for empty stimulation a painfully physical form.

Advertisement

In the show’s longest section, she has her two dancers –Billy Keohavong and Ko Yamada – compete in a game show parody. Tasks include walking barefoot over Lego and transporting apples without hands. The loser of each round must brush their teeth with wasabi paste. In skimpy black briefs – one with a motorcycle helmet, the other in goggles – they maintain an affectless formality while completing their set tasks. The dancers maintain an affectless formality while completing their set tasks. Daniel Boud Winning and losing barely register. Only suppressed grunts during the penalty reveal the human agent beneath this ridiculous ceremony. The other sections are more dancerly but just as absurd. In one extended duet, unison gradually becomes bodily fusion. Rolling together across the stage, their tangled limbs resolve into a creature with four crablike legs, scuttling across the stage with disconcerting agility.

Advertisement

The final section recreates the candied choreography of K-pop group Girls’ Generation’s 2009 hit Gee. Keohavong and Yamada perform it with impressive lightness and zip, their energy apparently undiminished by the punishing ordeal they have just endured. Editor's pick Visual art This artist wants you to leave her exhibition feeling odd – and ‘squished’ It’s a weirdly comforting note on which to end. Two well-built, barely clothed men performing such a saccharine routine is funny, but there is a kind of wistful nostalgia in this moment of looking back. A longing for what the internet was or perhaps might have become. This show completes the Orbit program at Dancehouse, which introduced a series of work from interstate. Its slickness and nearly naked physicality feel distinctly Sydney: a welcome encounter with another city’s dance culture – and a persuasive argument for more interstate touring.

Reviewed by Andrew Furhmann

Advertisement

MUSIC

The Trumpet of the Swan ★★★

Opera Australia, Regent Theatre, until November 22 What business does an opera company have in staging a show that is without any singing at all? It’s a valid question, though Jason Robert Brown’s “novel symphony for actors and orchestra” is certainly not undeserving of a performance by Opera Australia. Arjun Tiwari as Louis in Opera Australia’s The Trumpet of the Swan. Ben Fon Based on the 1970 book by E.B. White (author of Charlotte’s Web and Stuart Little), the plot follows a young trumpeter swan born without a voice, who is given a literal trumpet and, of course, his uniqueness becomes his greatest strength. It is a coming-of-age story, really. Best known as a Broadway composer (The Last Five Years, Songs for a New World), Jason Robert Brown’s music is highly accessible and melodic without ever being basic. Sydney-based conductor Chad Kelly does a superb job of guiding Orchestra Victoria through the many compositional styles, with a lightness and ease that exudes appropriate playfulness. OV principal trumpet Mark Fitzpatrick is the star of the night, his solos sonorous and charming.

Advertisement

Following his highly acclaimed production of Grey Gardens, director Tyran Parke brings to the national opera company an outstanding troupe of Australian stage and small screen talent. Ben Mingay, from whom charisma overfloweth, is delightfully boisterous as Father Swan; Bert LaBonté an affable guide as the Storyteller, while Marney McQueen and Grant Piro both dazzle with an array of humorous accents and physical comedy. As the mute swan, dancer Arjun Tiwari moves with nimble elegance. Arhun Tiwari as Louis and Ben Mingay as Father Swan Ben Fon It is a tricky thing to mount, children’s entertainment with classical-ish orchestra; the closest thing to Trumpet in the standard repertory is Prokofiev’s well-known and beloved Peter and the Wolf. But if this show is truly intended for kids, perhaps a longer rehearsal period to allow for the actors to be off-book, plus colourful costumes and lively puppetry would allow for this production to, for want of a better word, sing.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

MUSIC

Foo Fighters | Take Cover Tour ★★★★

Marvel Stadium, November 14 Welcome to Foo Fest 2026. Circle the belly of Marvel Stadium where bars, carnival-style cuisine and a robust smokers’ section swarm with Foo Fighters’ multigenerational fanbase. As the band takes the stage, charismatic master of dad rock Dave Grohl promises, firmly, to kick our asses with three hours of rock’n’roll. Dave Grohl is an impeccable frontman. Richard Clifford Female-fronted openers FRENZEE and The Belair Lip Bombs are a thoughtful balance to the masculinity marathon. Foo Fighters bear the weight of three hours – and 31 live-playing years – with power. Grohl is an impeccable frontman, who says f--- a lot, and motherf---er almost as much. His presence is amplified on towering screens, tracing neck muscles straining in each scream, chewing gum slipping between brilliantly bared teeth. Grohl swaggers with rockstar theatrics, flinging hair, chugging beer and breaking for wandering digressions that are charmingly, well, dad.

Advertisement

The production flashes with lightning-storm illumination and ever-changing video aesthetics: dreamy, distorted, scribble-scattered or bursting with colour. Even those at the back get one hell of a show. Classics deviate into fresh solos. The crowd collaborates, enunciating the anthemic Best of You and My Hero, stamping to the chugging riffs of Walk, carrying a constellation of phone lights in These Days. Foo Fighters has a muscular sound. Grohl can sustain screams but falters a little in quieter moments, straining for Under You, his melodies in This is a Call swallowed by guitar snarls and crashing drums. An exception is Aurora, played in honour of late drummer Taylor Hawkins, pensive sorrow-rock powered with gentle, earnest vocals. Ilan Rubin, Chris Shiflett and Pat Smear perform at Marvel Stadium on November 14, 2026. Richard Clifford Ilan Rubin is a captivating successor to Hawkins, from galloping beats and a mind-melting solo in No Son Of Mine to the hypnotic drive of Run. Drumroll attacks in Monkey Wrench are matched by frenzied cinematography, this possessed musical beast about to destroy himself. Grohl plays towards him, a mirroring of mop-haired, black-clad men. In the medley, they switch: Grohl smiling ecstatically in his old home at the kit, Rubin rippling out a guitar solo. Instruments enjoy clear definition in the medley: Nate Mendel’s bass momentum, Pat Smear and Chris Shiflett’s ringing guitar solos, Rami Jaffee’s bubbling keyboard. Audio clarity drifts throughout the show, at times slipping into muddiness.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
